In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole tackle the controversial topic of scruffing, while also sharing some fun comparisons between cats, dogs, and toddlers. Instead of treating scruffing like an absolute taboo, the hosts break down why understanding a cat's specific boundaries can make quick vet visits or home care way less stressful for everyone. Dr. Karyn brings her cat, Sirill, onto the desk to show why a timid pinch fails, how a solid hold gives cats a sense of security, and how to quickly test if your cat is way too sensitive for the technique.

Get the real scoop on scruffing catsâincluding why total bans ignore harm reduction when you just need to safely pull out a thorn or trim nails in a pinch. Dr. Karyn breaks down the biggest mistakes pet parents make, explaining why delicately pinching a bit of skin only annoys your cat and how a full-hand hold actually provides better control and stability. Youâll also learn how to check your catâs tolerance before even trying a hold so you never accidentally upset a sensitive pet.

Plus, the hosts chat about research comparing how dogs, cats, and toddlers help others, debating whether cats are truly selfish or just super selective about their time. From winning over shy rescue cats to comparing dogs to needy toddlers and cats to moody teenagers, this episode offers a relaxed, relatable look at living with felines.

Rethinking the Scruffing Debate: Dr. Karyn and Nicole discuss how complete anti-scruffing rules miss the mark on practical care. They explain that learning safe restraint acts as harm reduction, letting you handle fast tasks like pulling out a thorn or trimming claws without having to resort to full sedation.

Test Sensitivity First: Before going in for a hold, Dr. Karyn recommends checking the neck area with gentle pets and tickles. If a cat flinches or pulls away (like her cat, Zelda), you should never try to scruff them.

Skip the "Pinch": The most common mistake people make is grabbing a tiny pinch of skin, which just annoys the cat and provokes a fight. Proper restraint needs a full, firm hand on the scruff so the cat feels secure and can't wriggle free.

Never Pick Them Up by the Scruff: The hosts emphasize that while a hand on the scruff helps keep a cat grounded, you should never lift or carry an adult cat this way.

Altruism in Pets vs. Toddlers: The conversation turns to research comparing toddlers, dogs, and cats. Studies show dogs and kids will help out even without a reward, while cats generally step in only when thereâs something clear in it for them.

Earned Love Feels Extra Special: Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how dogs offer constant, people-pleasing affection, whereas a catâs love feels like an earned privilege. That conditional nature is exactly what makes it so rewarding when a quiet cat finally comes over to snuggle.

#8016. What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

Bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

Unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

Impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.

#8013. Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder Review 2026: Our Expert’s Opinion

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This review was created in partnership with Neakasa, who compensated us for our time and editorial work. However, our opinions and ratings remain entirely our ownâwe only recommend products we genuinely believe in, and all assessments reflect our honest experience and testing.

We give the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder a rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars.

Youâve probably heard by now that feeding wet food to your cat is better than feeding dry food. This has a lot to do with hydration and moisture levels. As it turns out, most cats donât drink enough water, and a diet of dry food compounds the issue by further dehydrating them.

Feeding canned or wet food is a great solution to this issue. Unless, of course, you travel, work long hours, or otherwise donât have the bandwidth to open can after can for your hungry feline.

This is where the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder comes in. This isnât another automatic wet cat food feeder that requires constant refilling and cleaning. Oh no, this is something completely new.

This revolutionary device fresh-grinds freeze-dried cat food, rehydrates it with filtered water, then serves it automaticallyâup to 20 meals per day! Never before has keeping your cat hydrated been so easy or so tasty.

But does this high-tech contraption live up to the hype? I had the opportunity to test this space-age automatic cat feeder with the help of my hungry-hippo kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to see what we liked about it and if itâs worth the purchase in my full Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder review.

Domestic cats are descended from African desert wild cats. These wild felines got most of their hydration from their prey. Their kidneys became ultra-efficient at retaining moisture, and their drive to find fresh water sources nearly disappeared completely.

Our house cats retain this same physiology and lack of interest in hunting down fresh water. The problem? They arenât typically chowing down on juicy rodents a dozen times a day. Which means they often donât get the moisture they need to keep those specialized kidneys healthy.

This is why 40% of cats over 10 years old and 80% of cats over 15 years old develop chronic kidney disease. After a lifetime of chronic dehydration, their kidneys simply canât keep up.

One solution is to increase the amount of water cats consume through their food by offering wet food or adding water to their dry food. This is doable if you are home during meal times every day. But if you work long hours, have a million other things to juggle, or occasionally (or often) travel, feeding moist meals consistently becomes more of a challenge.

Some turn to automatic wet food feeders that keep pre-prepared portions of wet food cool, automatically opening each portion on a set schedule. While these work in the short term, they hold only a limited amount of food (generally between three and six meals) and require a lot of cleanup and constant restocking.

For those who travel or already struggle to get everything done in a day, this is far from being a convenient or effective solution.

The Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder combines the health benefits of a wet-food diet with the convenience and high-capacity of a dry-food automatic feeder.

Unlike traditional automatic wet food feeders that can only store a handful of meals, the Neakasa Riko Fresh-Made Wet Meal Feeder can hold weeks of food at a time and dispense meals up to every hour, keeping kitties with even the most specialized dietary needs happy and hydrated throughout the day.

Rather than canned or wet packaged food, the Riko works with freeze-dried cat food. This shelf-stable food is ground up into portions, mixed with water, and allowed to rehydrate before serving.

No refrigeration or constant refilling needed. Just fill the hopper with a bag of freeze-dried food of your choice, add filtered water to the reservoir, set the amounts and feeding schedule on the app, and take a well-deserved break from fretting over your catâs meals and hydration status.

Neakasa is a smart-home and pet-care brand operated by Genhigh, a technology company headquartered in Shenzhen, China. Founded in 2017 as Neabot, the company specializes in automated solutions designed to make everyday home and pet care easier, including robotic cleaning and smart pet products. The Riko is manufactured in China, where the company is based.

Given the price point of this product, I wouldnât recommend it to cat owners simply hoping to unload some of their kitty chores to automation. There are less expensive automatic feeders for that. But for cat owners who normally feed wet food but are taking a long trip or frequently travel and want a feeder that can provide meals more often than their cat sitter can, the Riko Wet Meal Feeder is a worthwhile investment.

It is also a great option for cats who require small portions frequently throughout the day or who already eat freeze-dried food and can benefit from a more consistent schedule and more moisture in their diet.

Because this feeder allows for highly customized feeding routines and portions, it works well for kittens, adults, and seniors. But do be aware that the meal sizes cap out at 15g of dried food, which means larger cats may require multiple feedings throughout the day rather than the typical two meals they might be used to, something the app makes easy.

The Neakasa Riko takes the guesswork out of serving moistened meals. Simply fill the food hopper with compatible freeze-dried food, fill the water tank, and use the app to create a feeding schedule.

At mealtime, Riko automatically grinds the food, adds your selected amount of water, and allows the mixture to soak while the bowl is hidden out of reach. Once the food is ready, the bowl swings out so your cat can enjoy their fresh meal.

You can adjust the water-to-food ratio to create a consistency your cat prefers, from thicker to more soupy. Riko can schedule multiple meals throughout the day, add water to keep uneaten food fresh, and track food consumption through the app.

Beyond preparing moistened meals, the Riko packs several thoughtful features into the feeder itself:

Large capacity: The 3-liter food hopper and 2.4-liter water tank can hold enough for 10+ days of feeding.

Freshness-focused design: An airtight food compartment, desiccant system, and sealed grinder help protect freeze-dried food from moisture.

Precise portions: Riko weighs each serving for approximately Â±1-gram portioning.

Easy cleaning: The removable stainless-steel bowl is dishwasher-safe, while other components can be removed for cleaning. Each order comes with two bowls, so you can pop one in the dishwasher while the other is in use.

The Neakasa app gives you control over Riko from your phone, whether youâre home or away. You can create feeding schedules, adjust portion sizes and water-to-food ratios, and trigger extra meals remotely.

The app also records your catâs food and water intake, making it easier to spotchanges in eating habits over time. Youâll receive alerts for low food and water storage and potential feeding problems, while adjustable settings let you configure features such as freshness detection, child lock, and desiccant replacement reminders.

Through the app, you have control over the amount of ground food in each meal, the ratio of water added, how long it sits to rehydrate, and how often water is added if food is left over. You can even program âwater onlyâ meals to encourage even more moisture intake.

Riko can be customized with a few optional accessories. The rechargeable battery pack provides up to seven days of cordless operation and backup power during outages, while the Multi-Cat Access Module uses microchip recognition to restrict feeding to each designated cat in multi-cat households.

Neakasa also sells replacement silicone desiccant packs with a color-changing indicator that lets you know when the pack needs replacing.

Number of meals per fill: about 10 daysâ worth

Compatible with: most types of freeze-dried food

Number of meals per fill: 3 daysâ worth

Compatible with: all types of canned food

If youâve read any of my reviews before, then you know that my cat, Makoa, is a BIG fan of food. So any device that makes meal times less of a hassle for me and more accessible for him is worth trying out. And, since our family also travels fairly frequently, I thought this high-tech contraption might be helpful in multiple ways.

When the Riko arrived, I immediately felt like I was unboxing some kind of fancy kitty espresso maker! Itâs about the same size as one, and the grinder really does look very similar to a coffee grinder.

Getting the Riko set up was fairly painless. I followed the Quick Start Instructions to assemble the few parts that had been stored internally during shipping, then downloaded the app and connected the device to my Wi-Fi.

From there, things got a touch trickier. Because the Riko works using weight, not volume, it can be a little difficult to set the proportions for each meal. For example, I typically feed Makoa Â¼ cup twice per day. How many grams of ground freeze-dried food plus water is that? No idea.

Luckily, the app does have a very helpful Smart Feeding Plan setup that allows you to use your catâs weight and select the type of food you feed to automatically create a feeding schedule based on the food brand's recommended intake.

The downside here is that it defaults to 10 meals per day. Which probably isnât a bad thing since cats did evolve to eat multiple small meals throughout the day (and this also guarantees better hydration). But if your cat is used to a couple of big meals at the same time each day, this can make for a tough transition.

I ended up manually adding up the dry food total it recommended, then manually adding meals that were more aligned with his typical schedule.

The other hangup I ran into is that the feeder (in the US, at least) maxes out at 15g of ground food per meal. For comparison, my 12-pound cat needs about 60g of ground food per day. In other words, I had to schedule at least four meals per day for him to get all the food he needs.

These smaller meal sizes are intentional. Not only does it help avoid food being wasted (or left out for too long without being eaten), but it also ensures your cat is continually taking in food-based moisture throughout the dayâthe way they evolved to.

So I wouldnât say this is a bad thing or design flaw, but it is something you and your cat may need to adjust to.

Beyond the tricky parts of portioning and scheduling, I really do love this feeder! It is so easy to fill and, once the schedule is set, you really can just forget it. It starts preparing each meal ahead of time so that the food is ready at the scheduled mealtime.

It makes a recognizable beep when food is ready, so your cat can learn to come as soon as dinner is served. (Makoa learned to recognize the low buzz of the grinder almost instantly, and now waits for his meals twenty minutes before they are served.)

Not only has this gadget taken the stress off me (now Makoa has something else to obsess over when itâs dinner time), but it has made it so much easier to ensure consistent, moist meals throughout the day. And I know it will be a lifesaver for those weekend trips and long vacations our family likes to go on.

I highly recommend this feeder to anyone who is looking for a way to automate their catâs meals without having to rely on dry kibble. The rehydrated freeze-dried food isnât the same as canned food, but the texture is similar, and most cats love this type of food, especially when it is mixed with water. Even better, freeze-dried food tends to be healthier and more nutrient-dense than even the best canned food options.

No. Riko is designed to grind and rehydrate freeze-dried food, not conventional wet food. Do not put canned, pouch, or other wet food, or kibble, dehydrated, or air-dried food into the hopper.

Riko's smart features and remote app controls require a Wi-Fi connection, but once programmed, the feeder can still perform its feeding schedule if the internet connection is interrupted. It supports 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi networks.

Because Riko adds water to the food before serving, the resulting meal should be treated like wet food. Neakasa recommends that your cat consume it within about three to four hours.

Riko's freshness settings can detect leftover food and pause the next scheduled feeding when the amount remaining exceeds your chosen threshold. The feeder can also retract the bowl after food has remained uneaten for an extended period.

If hydration is a concern for your cat and providing consistent moist food is a challenge for you, then the Neakasa Riko is worth looking into.

This high-tech automatic feeder can store 10 days' worth of freeze-dried food at a time and provide up to 20 freshly rehydrated meals per day. Each meal can be scheduled and proportioned to meet your catâs needs while ensuring their moisture intake is optimal to avoid future health issues. It's perfect for busy cat parents, extended periods away, and cats who require frequent, moistened meals.

Plenty of garden pests spend winter as eggs or dormant adults in old vines, twigs, and leaves. Remove them during fall cleanup – but spare the helpful insects.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By late October, the vegetable beds are mostly dead vines, and the shrubs are dropping leaves. At that point, fall cleanup is usually just tidying up. Next year's garden pests are still in that mess, though. Squash bugs shelter under the old vines, moths leave egg masses on bark and lawn chairs, and beetles seal their eggs inside viburnum twigs.

Many common garden pests don't die off in winter. They spend it as eggs, pupae, or dormant adults in one spot, and they mostly stay there until spring. That makes them pretty easy to find and remove right now. A pair of pruners, a putty knife, or a rake can take out a whole tent caterpillar colony before it ever hatches.

Where you look depends on the pest. Some hide their eggs inside twigs, while others leave them right out on bark or a fence post. A few of the egg cases and cocoons you'll find belong to beneficial insects, though, and those should stay put.

Insects that overwinter usually ride out the cold in a resting stage. For a lot of garden pests, that means an egg mass on a twig, a pupa in the soil, or an adult wedged under leaf litter. Eggs and pupae can't scatter, and dormant adults barely move. Bare branches help too – egg masses hidden by summer foliage are much easier to spot once the leaves fall. One scraped egg mass in October can mean hundreds fewer caterpillars in spring.

So why not rake up everything? Good insects spend the winter in the same spots as the bad ones. Lady beetles and ground beetles burrow into leaf litter, and many native bees tuck into hollow stems. Strip every bed bare during fall cleanup, and those go, too. Focus on whatever had problems this year, and leave the rest a little messy.

Here's where some common pests spend the winter and how to clear them out.

Squash bugs (Anasa tristis) are still around after the plants die. Adults crawl under dead vines and leaf litter for the winter, and some hide under nearby boards. Clear that out once the squash and pumpkins are done. Those vines are prickly, so you'll need good protective gloves like these nitrile-coated garden gloves from Home Depot. Bag the vines rather than piling them up, or the bugs move right in.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your viburnums got chewed up this summer, the leaf beetles (Pyrrhalta viburni) probably left eggs in the twigs. You won't see the eggs, just little rows of bumps near the tips of this year's branches once the leaves are off. Those are the caps the females made from chewed bark. Cut the twigs off with sharp bypass pruning shears (these Fiskars bypass pruners on Amazon are good value for money if you need a new pair) and trash them before spring.

Eastern tent caterpillars (Malacosoma americanum) mostly feed on cherry and apple trees, so start there. Look along the thin twigs for a shiny black band, like someone dripped varnish around the branch. That's the egg mass. Snip the twig off or crush the band, and throw it out. For a big tree, Monterey horticultural oil works as a late-winter dormant spray that can smother the eggs.

Anyone in the Northeast or upper Midwest has likely heard of spongy moth (Lymantria dispar), once called gypsy moth. Its caterpillars can strip a tree bare in a bad year. Right now, though, they're just eggs, packed by the hundreds into tan, fuzzy patches on tree trunks and fences. Check sheds and the underside of patio chairs, too. Scrape each patch into a bucket of soapy water – a soft-sided tub like this Tubtrugs one from Walmart works well – and let it soak for several days.

Iris borer moths (Macronoctua onusta) lay their eggs on old iris leaves in late summer and early fall, and the eggs wait there until spring. Then the caterpillars hatch, climb the new leaves, and tunnel down into the rhizome. Wait until after a hard frost, since the moths can keep laying until then, and cut away the old leaves. Dispose of the foliage in the trash rather than adding it to your compost pile.

If you've had trouble with iris borers before, consider keeping a spinosad-based insecticide, such as Bonide Captain Jack's Deadbug Brew, on hand for spring, when newly hatched caterpillars are vulnerable to treatment before they burrow into the rhizomes.

Scale insects (Coccoidea) stay stuck to the stems and branches of shrubs and trees all winter. They look like small bumps that come off with a scrape of a fingernail. It could be an adult female, a young one, or a cover with eggs under it, depending on the type of scale. Scrub off what you can, and treat the tiny crawlers with Garden Safe insecticidal soap, available on Amazon. Look over potted citrus before bringing it inside, since scale can keep breeding indoors.

Plenty of aphids (Aphididae) get through winter as eggs on rose canes and fruit tree twigs, especially on apples. Those eggs are tiny, black, and shiny, and they're usually near a bud or in a crack in the bark. They're hard to see without a 10x handheld magnifier, like this one with a built-in light on Amazon. Winter pruning gets rid of many, and a dormant oil spray before the buds start to swell can kill more. If some still hatch, a spray of Bonide neem oil from Walmart can help.

Lady beetles, lacewings, mantises, butterflies, and native bees overwinter in the garden too. Don't remove these beneficial insects.

Lady beetles tend to bunch up in winter, and raking into the leaves at the base of a tree can turn up a whole cluster. Cover them back up and move on. Both adults and larvae eat aphids, and every beetle that survives the winter is one more working the garden next year.

Mantis egg cases look like dried globs of tan foam, sometimes as big as a golf ball, glued to a stem or twig. If one is on a stem, you need to cut below the case and tuck the stem into a shrub, off the ground. Mantises do eat helpful insects, too.

Lacewing eggs are easy to recognize – each one perches on the tip of a hair-thin silk stalk. By fall, you're more likely to find the round, papery cocoons that larvae spin in hidden spots on plants, or adults sheltering in leaf litter. The larvae are voracious aphid predators. Leave both stages in place.

Black swallowtail caterpillars spend the summer eating parsley and dill, and the last ones of the year don't leave in fall – they hang on through winter as brown chrysalises, sometimes on the old herb stems. One looks a lot like a scrap of dead plant, so go slowly when you cut those herbs back.

Native bees need a winter spot, too. Many of them nest in the ground, and bare soil is easier to dig into than mulch. Leave a patch or two uncovered. Other bees use hollow or pithy stems like raspberry canes, and their young spend the winter sealed inside. Leave those stems standing until spring warms up, then cut them back to about knee height.

A clean garden and a healthy garden aren't always the same thing. Cut the marked twigs, scrape the egg masses, and clear out the old squash vines and iris leaves. Then let the rest of the leaves lie. Next spring should bring fewer squash bugs and more lady beetles.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Meet Dave Coverly, creator of the popular cartoon panel, âSpeed Bumpâ, which appears internationally in hundreds of publications, including The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and the Detroit Free Press. His work was named âBest in Newspaper Panelsâ by the National Cartoonists Society in 1995, 2003, 2014, and 2021. He is also the principal cartoonist for Bark (formerly BarkBox) and illustrator for Ranger Rick magazine.

We sit down with Dave to learn the story behind his charmingly wry comic, and find out how, 32 years down the road, inspiration in the ordinary keeps his content relevant and relatable.

The path to becoming a professional cartoonist always starts in childhood â pretty much every kid likes to draw, right? And I was no different. But as kids get older, they tend to get more particular about how good their drawings look, and thatâs where frustration sets in. They tend to move on to other hobbies. Where a cartoonistâs path diverges from that of wiser, more sensible humans is that we love the process of creating more than we chafe at the frustration. Believe me, there is frustration. One misconception about artists is that we do it because it comes easy to us, but the general truth is that most of us put in long hours because we want to be good at what we already love.

I taped rejection letters to the wall above my drawing table for motivation. At the time, though, my panels didnât have a title, so when my breakthrough finally happened, I needed to name it. I submitted a list of possible titles to Creators, and Speed Bump was the unanimous choice. Fortunately, that was my top choice, too. Iâd like people to perhaps slow down just for a second when they read my work since Iâm rarely going to hit you over the head with the joke.

My second favorite title was The Wide World of Stretch Pants.

Animal humor has always been a part of my work. I was slightly obsessed with Ranger Rick magazine growing up, and spent loads of time drawing the critters they featured. I discovered thereâs something inherently funny and absurd about talking animals, not to mention itâs the most fun way to trigger the imagination. What would a giraffe order at a restaurant? What does a dolphin dream about? That was how I discovered how much fun cartooning was â and that the crazier you make it, the less perfect it needs to be.

Iâve always had a dog until very recently, and had two hilarious knuckleheads as a kid: Shag and Tigger. They were actually father and son, and I didnât need a DNA test to prove it â Shag got out one day, and the neighborhood kids on bikes came by to let me know he could be found down the street at Queenieâs house, where they were in the front yard together. Letâs just say Shag was living up to his name. Then Queenie begat Tigger.

I grew up in a small lake community, but Shag was found by my grandpa just living on the streets of Detroit. He was pretty feral â Shag, not my grandpa â and impossible to train, but also a total sweetheart. They slept in the garage, and in the morning weâd often find him sleeping on top of the car. Tigger, on the other hand, preferred to sleep behind the toilet. And he wasnât a small dog.

In any case, I believe these two funny mutts had as much influence on my work as any other cartoonist.

Great question! Cats and dogs are obviously very different, but they have one really big thing in common: their own unique personalities. Thatâs what makes both perfect for cartoons â most of us already treat them like little furry people anyway, right? Itâs just their behaviors that set them apart.

Dogs tend to be goofier, cats tend to be cooler, and they show affection in their own ways, too. Pets generate a lot of material because almost everyone knows a dog or a cat. Even if they donât have one (or many) themselves, the odds are a reader will recognize why the cartoon is funny (hopefully!).

One of my most popular cartoons is a sign that says âBeware of Avant-Guard Dog,â and the dog in the yard is wearing black and a beret and holding a sign simply saying WOOF. The idea started as a pun, but I think one of the reasons readers seem to like it so much is that it plays against type. The dogâs sensibility is quite cat-like, making it even more absurd.

My new book is a full-color collection of the âbest ofâ my dog cartoons from the last decade, and thereâs only one cartoon per page so that they can be seen in a larger format, which was important to me. I put a lot of effort into the art and the details, things that are often lost when the cartoons are shrunk down to an illegible size, so I wanted readers to be able to fully enjoy that aspect of the cartoons. Also, the friend who colors my panels, Ron Raff, is a genius, so whether you think the jokes are funny or not, youâll see that they look gorgeous and consistent throughout!

It was difficult but fun to choose which cartoons made the cut, too. Some are simply personal favorites; others were chosen based on readersâ reactions and how much love they got online. Feedback is extremely helpful, by the way â sometimes it feels like Iâm drawing these alone in my belfry studio and tossing them into a black hole, so hearing from people which ones they liked really makes my day.

There are two aspects to dog cartoons: The first and most obvious is that they really arejokes about dogsâ behavior in general â how they eat, how they might react in different settings, why they lick themselves, bathroom habits, etc etc. Thereâs a lot of material there! The second aspect is what generates even more material, and thatâs when dogs are reflecting human behavior, or simply behaving like a human.

Many of the dog cartoons are really about us, and heaven knows people will never stop providing fodder for jokes. Dogs â and animals in general â are a good buffer between the joke and the point of the joke. A good example in the book is a dog shaking a toy in his mouth, and a woman next to him is saying, âBad dog! Drop Mommyâs voodoo doll! Bad dog!â In the background, her husband (presumably) shakes back and forth like the toy. At some level, the cartoon is about the coupleâs relationship, right? But itâs framed by a typical and humorous dog action weâve all seen before. Just not with a voodoo doll, haha.

I would say simply that our question is also the answer: love. I try to approach my cartoons the same way I approach dogs in real life; from a standpoint of love, affection, admiration, and a little bit of gratitude that they exist.

There have been too many to count over three decades! I drew a cartoon years ago of a man walking his dog in heaven, but the leash is attached to the dogâs halo. A few weeks later, I received a card in the mail from a woman whose dog had just passed awayâ¦only a month after her husband. She said she cried with happiness thinking of the two of them like that, and it made her heart feel lighter. How incredibly moving is that? I think of that often: when I share a cartoon, the reader brings their own life experiences to it and then weâve made a two-way connection. That connection is my favorite part of the gig.

My only hope is that my cartoons help people simply see the world in a different way for a few seconds. I want them to laugh with others and not at others; see that absurdities are universal and that when we recognize ourselves or others in a cartoon, weâre really just acknowledging that weâre all connected.

And then I hope they cut them out and slap them on their fridges.

The best place to find all my work and links is my site: www.speedbump.com, and anyone should feel free to reach out, follow, etc on Instagram (https://www.instagram.com/speedbumpcomic/) or Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/davecoverly)

If youâre a skywriter, aim for the west side of Ann Arbor. Iâll look out the skylight in my belfry studio.

His work was named âBest in Newspaper Panelsâ by the National Cartoonists Society in 1995, 2003, 2014 and 2021. In 2009 the same organization gave him its highest honor, the Reuben Award, for âOutstanding Cartoonist of the Yearâ.

Coverlyâs cartoons have also appeared in The New Yorker, USA Today, The New York Times, Newsweek and were a regular feature in Parade. According to local lore, Isobel Rorison and Dominick French’s English countryside home once served as a rest stop for monks making the pilgrimage between Glastonbury and Sherborne Abbey. That’s why the couple lovingly refers to the stone abode (parts of which date back to the 1380s) as The Priests’ House—though it also functioned as a dairy, a farmhouse, and an ex-ambassador’s residence throughout the centuries. Most recently, Dominick’s mother had been the historic home’s steward and had made few updates in her 40 years there. So when he and Isobel took the reins after her passing, they promptly decided a kitchen renovation was in order.

“We opened up the bottom floor to what would’ve been the original layout when it was built, which actually fits perfectly with modern living,” says Isobel. “Since it’s Grade II* listed, we couldn’t move anything else. There are two walls of windows and one with a huge fireplace, so that only left one wall for cabinets.”

With the floor plan set, Isobel and Dominick considered the aesthetic direction for their old/new cookspace. Thinking that ornate, Victorian-style cupboards would clash with the medieval wood beams and stonework, the duo opted for minimalist custom cabinetry by Husk, with clean-lined flat Fenix fronts that highlight the rustic original features. As for the palette? The couple chose muted hues of rusty red, dusty blue, and gray-green because they would’ve existed in the 15th century, when this section of the house was constructed.

#8009. Maitake: The Expensive Mushroom You Can Forage for Free

In the Northeast, October is a special month. As red maples begin to blaze, maitake, a prized edible mushroom, appears at the base of some old hardwood trees (which it is slowly killing). Favoring oak, the dense, heavy mushrooms may be nestled against the tree’s trunk, or a few feet away, fruiting from—and feeding on—old roots. The mushrooms reappear on the same trees year after year. And they are exceptionally good to eat. It is my twelfth season of hunting maitake in the wilds of New York City, and the sense of fun has not diminished.

Here’s where to find maitake, how to cook them, and some precautions to bear in mind.

The name maitake means “dancing mushroom” in Japanese. It is very hard to control the excited wiggle in your walk as you approach the first mushroom of the season, and your next dinner. Maitake grow in temperate forests in the Northern Hemisphere, favoring cold winters and old hardwoods, and they do not differentiate between rural and urban forests. In cities you might even spot them on street trees.

Maitake is also known as hen of the woods: picture a fluffed-out gray hen sitting on her brood.

Oak trees are maitake’s usual host, and I have also seen them at the base of beeches, cherry, and even a London plane. The mushroom is parasitic, feeding on the trees’ roots, and causing a white rot, which will weaken its benefactor and contribute eventually to so-called tip-over (when a tree topples from the base).

While immature mushrooms can fit in the palm of your hand, grown-up maitake can weigh upwards of 10 pounds and sometimes double that. It is hard not to feel pleased carrying home such a prize on your way past a gourmet store charging upwards of $20/lb for foraged maitake. They are cultivated, too, a process pioneered by Japanese growers. These tame mushrooms look very different from their feral cousins: small, delicate, and frilly, versus sturdy and heavy. Their flavor is milder, although quite good.

Maitake appearing in carpets of fallen leaves are cleaner than those surrounded by bare soil, which splashes up if there is rain and is incorporated in the mushroom as it grows, making it gritty to chew. Use a sharp knife to slice the maitake at the base, trimming off any debris stuck to the bottom. Avoid mushrooms growing at the base of trees used by raccoons as a latrine (there will be tell-tale signs of scat). And always cook your wild-collected mushrooms.

What part of wild maitake is best to eat? In a young, butter-tender mushroom, the whole mushroom is delicious, cooked. On larger maitake, the gray caps, or “feathers” remain tender.

At home, slice smaller maitake in half to see how clean they are. Trim away any debris, and wash. For  tender mushrooms, you can also tear the caps, keeping a strand of the soft white core attached to each. Then wash.

For large mushrooms, cut off the caps for dinner and save the woody core to roast for broth.

In terms of flavor and fragrance maitake is exceptional. While the mushroom cooks, especially if it is roasted, the scent is—at least to my nose—reminiscent of chestnut honey. When I first made maitake chips that first bite was a revelation: It tasted as though the mushroom had been marinated in soy sauce. Maitake contains l-glutamate, a natural flavor-enhancer, and the embodiment of umami.

Two layers of maitake complexity make this woodsy pilaf sing autumn. The woodier heart makes a flavorful broth, while the roasted ears  intensify that unique flavor. (I soak the farro for 72 hours; the resulting texture of the grain, which will have begun to sprout, is wonderful.) The recipe doubles easily.

Broth: In a saucepan over medium-high heat warm the oil and add the maitake heart. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the onion, garlic, and carrots, stir well and cook for another 5 minutes. Add the wine, water, salt, sugar, and pepper. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat to cook at a simmer for 40 minutes. Strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve. Measure out 1 cup for the pilaf (use the extra for soup, sauce, or just do broth shots!).

Roast mushrooms: Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F. In a bowl toss the maitake caps with the oil and salt. Transfer to a large skillet and into the oven. Roast for 40 to 45 minutes; they should be turning crisp and smelling good. Remove from the oven, take out the mushrooms and reserve, leaving the mushroom-infused in the skillet.

To finish: Place the skillet over medium heat and add the farro with the chives, stirring for a minute. The grains will make appealing, popping noises. Push the farro to one side and add the nuts. Leave them to toast for a minute then stir everything together (you will notice that the germ of the farro is showing up whitely at the tip of each grain, now). Toast together for another minute and then pour in all the broth. Bring to a gentle boil and cook, simmering, until it has all been absorbed, about 20 minutes. Taste. Add salt. Now stir in the roasted mushrooms, and give them a minute to heat through. Serve at once.

(Although it is completely unnecessary no one has ever turned down the offer of some microplaned parmesan over the top…)

N.B.: This post has been updated; it was first published October 2022.

#8008. PetPivot AutoScooper 12 Review 2026: Our Expert Opinion

This review was created in partnership with PetPivot, who compensated us for our time and editorial work. However, our opinions and ratings remain entirely our own. We only recommend products we genuinely believe in, and all assessments reflect our honest experience and testing.

We give the PetPivot AutoScooper 12 4.9 out of 5 stars.

2026 has not been everyoneâs favorite year, but for me and my cats, there has been one thing that has put it on the map: upgrading to a self-cleaning litter box. Despite living with five cats, I had written off the idea of having an automatic litter box as an unnecessary luxury. An expense I could never quite justify. When I was given the opportunity to try one out earlier this year, I discovered that not only can you pick up an excellent self-cleaning litter box for a very reasonable price, but they are not a luxury item. They are a necessity.

Although I deeply regret not buying one years ago, one benefit of waiting is that there are now more options, better designs, and lower prices than ever before. This is particularly true when it comes to the PetPivot AutoScooper 12, and as I discovered, there is more than meets the eye with this compact and quiet unit.

Ever since we started inviting cats into our homes, humans have been looking for better ways to deal with the unavoidable issue of their waste. Cats are fastidiously clean by nature, and teaching them to use a litter box is usually pretty straightforward. Keeping that litter box clean is decidedly more labor-intensive.

Maintaining good litter box hygiene isnât just about controlling odors. Some cats will happily share a litter box, while others will refuse to use soiled litter, even if they are the only cat using it. Inappropriate toileting â that is, peeing or pooping in shoes, on bedding, in fruit bowls(!) â can be a sign of a health problem, but more often than not, itâs about the litter box itself. The wrong location, the wrong type of litter, and most significantly, a box that isnât clean.

Unless youâre on standby, litter scooper in hand, all day every day, there will be times that your cat visits the litter box before youâve had a chance to clean it. And if, like me, you have more than one feline in the family, youâve likely got multiple litter boxes that you spend an immeasurable amount of time scooping, sifting, and cleaning.

One of the reasons I put off getting a self-cleaning litter box for so long was that I felt like it was something that would only benefit me. Donât get me wrong â it most definitely has! But now I realize how much it has also improved the lives of my cats. Instead of having to wait for me to provide them with a fresh tray, the automatic cleaning function means every cat gets a clean litter box for every visit.

Not having to scoop out litter boxes every day has been a total game-changer for me, and while itâs hard to put a price on how much my catsâ quality of life has improved, itâs nice to know that, at less than $150, the PetPivot Autoscooper 12 is well within reach of most pet owners.

The Autoscooper 12 is the newest self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot. The US company was founded in Portland, Oregon, in 2023. Following the overwhelming success of the AutoScooper 11, PetPivot released the new model in 2026, which is available in the US, Europe, the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, and Australia.

The AutoScooper 12 is a quieter, more compact unit that features upgraded motion sensors for improved safety and accuracy, and an integrated step that provides easier access for smaller cats or those with mobility issues.

If youâre worried that an open litter box means more litter tracking and unpleasant odors, donât be. The deep placement of the tray and the odor-locking design of the waste drawer minimizes litter scatter and keeps bad smells well-contained.

The litter tray contains a removable mat made from durable, water-resistant 300D Oxford fabric that minimizes âlitter stickâ and makes cleaning a breeze. For the most part, routine cleaning of the AutoScooper 12 consists of emptying the waste drawer once or twice a week (depending on the number of cats using it) and brushing any stray litter from around the unit. No more daily scooping. You will occasionally need to give the whole unit a proper clean, but itâs a relatively painless process.

Compared with the previous model, the AutoScooper 12 takes up less floor space, but also has a slightly smaller tray, which some particularly large or messy cats may struggle with. However, the open design provides most cats with plenty of room to move, and with an operating volume of 32 dB, itâs perfect for smaller spaces and apartment living.

In terms of function and design, the AutoScooper 12 is up there with the best, at a fraction of the price. Plus, it comes in a range of different colors, including pink!

The AutoScooper 12 comes with everything you need to get started:

You can also purchase extra rolls of waste drawer liners, litter tray mats, and PetPivotâs own PoPoLitter.

Iâd also recommend picking up a litter-trapping mat to place under the litter box to minimize litter tracking even further.

You can purchase the AutoScooper 12 and accessories directly from the PetPivot website. It comes with a 12-month limited warranty as standard, and when buying directly from the PetPivot website, you can add up to 3 years of accident protection for a very low price.

The AutoScooper 12 is also available from major retailers including Chewy, Amazon, and Walmart.

At the time of writing, the AutoScooper 12 is only $149, with additional discounts available from the website.

Thatâs right â a self-cleaning litter box for less than $150!

But as I discovered, low cost does not mean low quality.

As they like to say, this isnât my first rodeo, and having already been converted to the wonders of a self-cleaning litter box, I felt particularly qualified to assess this latest offering from PetPivot.

Unlike my other unit, the AutoScooper 12 arrived virtually fully assembled, and once Iâd unpacked the various components from their boxes or bags, I only needed to attach the legs, insert a liner into the waste tray, and attach the step to the front. Add some clumping bentonite-clay litter and presto! With a tray area of 12â x 14â, the AutoScooper 12 is quite a bit smaller than my 15â x 16â unit, but the actual litter volume capacity is quite similar, so this will only be an issue if you have particularly large cats.

Being naturally curious and experienced automatic litter box users, my cats wasted no time becoming intimately familiar with their shiny new toilet, and the AutoScooper 12 is even quieter than the one I already have! When given the option of using their old top-entry, enclosed litter box, all five cats chose the open-topped AutoScooper every time.

One thing I did notice is that while my other unit will pause mid-cycle if you look at it wrong, the AutoScooper 12 is not quite as sensitive. This could raise flags about safety, but the design of the AutoScooper 12 means that there is only one point towards the end of the cleaning cycle where a gap large enough for a cat appears. Any motion in the area at this stage paused the cycle immediately.

To allow waste storage, self-cleaning litter boxes are unavoidably tall, and I really like how the AutoScooperâs step latches onto the waste drawer. I particularly liked that the waste drawer came out the front, unlike my other unit where I have to shimmy things around to open it from the side.

The waste tray capacity is very impressive, and after a week (used alongside my other litter box), the AutoScooper 12 was holding around 6.4 lbs (2.9kg) of soiled litter and waste, compared with 5.7 lbs (2.6kg) in the other unit. That means more days without having to perform litter box duties. If used on its own with a single cat, I would estimate that it would take at least 10-14 days for the waste drawer to register as full. However, it is recommended that you empty the drawer every 5-7 days, depending on conditions, to avoid odors, mould, and flies.

Imagine going from daily sifting and scooping to just ditching a bag of used kitty litter one or twice a week â It is bliss.

There were only a couple of things I was a bit bummed about with the AutoScooper 12. Not having an alternative litter guard option to allow the use of long-fiber cat litters like tofu is a shame, particularly as these more eco-friendly materials are becoming more popular.

Another slight design flaw is that litter and debris accumulate around the top of the tray where the liner meets the unit, and need to be dislodged with a brush.

Overall, I think the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot is a really nice little unit, particularly for the price. It could be a tad small if youâve got a big Maine Coon or similarly large breed of cat, but for everyone else, the compact size means you wonât struggle to find space to accommodate it.

If youâre on the fence about getting a self-cleaning litter box, but arenât sure if your budget can stretch to such luxuries, itâs time to check out the AutoScooper 12 from PetPivot. Your cats deserve it, and so do you. And at this price, an automatic litter box isnât just wishful thinking; it belongs on next weekâs shopping list.

PetPivot recommends only clay, mineral, or bentonite clumping cat litter. Crystal litter, non-clumping litter, or materials with long pieces like tofu litter are not suitable.

PetPivot advises that the unit is only suitable for cats over 6 months and weighing over 3 lbs. However, you can switch the unit to manual mode or keep it turned off to allow younger kittens to get used to it.

Yes! Although the litter tray sits at around 10 inches tall, the removable 6-inch step makes entry and exit easier for older cats.

The AutoScooper 12 comes with a 30-day return policy (unused units only) and a 12-month limited warranty. You can also purchase up to 3 years of accident protection when you buy from the PetPivot website.

The AutoScooper 12 is manufactured in China. PetPivot is a US-owned and operated company.

Every cat should have access to a clean litter box, and one of the most important parts of being a responsible cat parent is making sure that happens. Itâs also one of the most tedious parts, which is why weâre all very grateful to an engineer named Brad Baxter, inventor of the automatic litter box. For most of us, however, these technological wonders have long been seen as luxury items that only the super-rich could afford.

The compact & stylish AutoScooper 12 proves that those days are well and truly over.

This self-cleaning litter box from PetPivot is quiet, easy to use, and is more than a match for units that cost five or six times its price. So unless you love the daily drudgery of scooping out the litter box, go out and treat yourself to an AutoScooper 12 â you wonât regret it.

#8007. Thinking About Adopting A Dog? Here Are 5 Things To Ask Before Bringing Them Home

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

This article was created in sponsorship with Mars, which helps make content like this possible.

Adopting can be one of the most rewarding ways to welcome a new pet into your life. But for many would-be adopters, the biggest hurdle isnât necessarily that they don't want to adopt; it's feeling confident that theyâre making an informed and responsible decision.

Mars research found that while 58% of pet owners have never adopted from a shelter or rescue organization, nearly a third would consider it with the right support available. Whether you have concerns about a pet's medical and behavior history, or understanding what to feed them, there are lots of questions to consider before welcoming a new dog into your home.

Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective and new dog owners access to practical, expert-backed support throughout the journey.

Responsible adoption is about more than picking the right dog; it's about making sure you can realistically meet their needs. Before adopting, think about your living space, daily routine, work arrangements, and how much time you can dedicate to helping your new dog settle in and meeting their exercise, enrichment, and training needs.

Surprising for some, living in an apartment, for example, does not automatically mean you cannot adopt a dog. The right match depends less on the size of your home and more on whether you can meet that individual dogâs physical, mental, and social needs.

Always mention if you have existing pets or children at the beginning of the adoption process too. Shelter staff can help identify pets whose personality, energy level, and other needs may be a good fit for family life.

The more you speak honestly and openly with the shelter about your home, family, and daily routine, the more they can help you understand which dog will be the right match.

Moving from a shelter into a home is a huge change for your new best friend, and youâd be amazed by how many dogs are returned to shelters within their first few days, before theyâve even had a chance to decompress, let alone adjust to their new situation.

A useful way to think about the transition is the â3-3-3â guideline: the first three days, three weeks, and three months.

During the first three days, your dog may feel overwhelmed. Dogs may hide, sleep more than usual, show less interest in food, or simply seem unsure of their surroundings. Some dogs may even show signs of fear or defensiveness, and itâs important to understand that this is not necessarily their true personality.

Keep things calm and predictable, and let your dog set the pace.

Once they become more comfortable, you may start seeing more of their personality from around three weeks, and this can be a good time to introduce gentle routines, socialization, and basic training. By around three months, many dogs may feel much more at home, although every pet is different, so donât worry if your dog seems to need longer. Just be patient and give them the time and space they need to feel safe.

Mars research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet immediately after adoption. However, switching your new dogâs food right away may not be the best option, even if their previous diet wasnât the best quality. Ask the shelter what your dog currently eats, how much they are fed, and how often. Keeping their existing food and routine initially can help reduce unnecessary disruption.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new diet to the dogâs regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest.

Puppies in particular need age-appropriate nutrition to support growth and should not be switched onto adult food too early.

A dogâs diet should be complete and balanced for their age, size, activity level, body condition and health needs, and plenty of fresh water should always be available.

Consistency can help your dog understand their new environment and build trust.

Establish regular times for meals, walks, rest, and play. As your dog becomes more comfortable, you can begin introducing basic training using positive reinforcement. Keep sessions short, fun, and rewarding.

Itâs normal for there to be some bumps along the way as your dog adjusts to a new home and routine. Behaviors they had previously learned â toilet training, for example â may temporarily change while they settle in, so patience and consistency are important.

If you notice any sudden, persistent, or concerning changes in behavior, speak to your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for advice.

Adopting and bringing a new dog home is just the beginning, and itâs completely normal for questions to come up as they settle into a new routine. If you need extra guidance regarding their behavior, health, nutrition, or day-to-day care, donât be afraid to reach out. Your shelter, veterinarian, or a qualified behavior professional can help you understand the right way forward.

For more advice to help you prepare for adoption and support your dog once theyâre home, visit the Mars Adoption Hub.

“In recent years, we’ve seen retail drift into a sort of sameness,” write Nancy and Kimberly Wu. “Building Block Etc. is our way back to meaning—a space for connection, where relationships happen face-to-face, and where you might hold something in your hands before choosing to make it part of your life.” The sisters are both industrial designers who studied at the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena and had impressive corporate careers before teaming up. Kim was a car concept designer for Honda in Tokyo and Nancy worked on performance footwear for Nike in Portland. They’re first generation Taiwanese-Americans, raised in Southern California—their father is an engineer—and after moonlighting long distance on their own designs, they returned home to their parents’ house in Orange County to launch Building Block.

That was back in 2011—the sisters were 25 and 27—and the brand started as a collection of five geometric handbags that attracted a cult following. It led to a successful shop and workshop in LA’s Chinatown, where the line expanded to include housewares. In 2023, Kimberly and Nancy transitioned their business into a creative consultancy, Studio Building Block, offering industrial design solutions. And more recently, they opened Building Block Etc., a shop showcasing a tightly edited array of their own designs and work by fellow maker friends. Explains Nancy, “we’re drawn to pieces that have clarity in material and form, a sense of utility, and the ability to reveal more over time.”

Photography courtesy of Building Block Etc. (@buildingblock).

Building Block Etc. is at 3021 Rowena Ave. in Silver Lake; it’s open Wed.–Sun., 11-5.

#8004. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Orphaned Kittens Are Suckling Each Other! (October 19, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

Our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their important social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â

Most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are currently targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

Keeping a bird bath ice-free could mean life or death for your garden birds this winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we head further into fall, it’s time to take steps to stop a bird bath freezing over and depriving birds of this valuable resource. Birds need daily access to water and when natural sources freeze over, a bird bath can become a vital lifeline and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard. During a cold snap, dehydration kills birds far faster than starvation, so keeping an ice-free bird bath this winter really is a lifesaver.

Water is surprisingly necessary to so many elements of avian survival in winter, and most small garden birds must drink at least once a day simply to stay alive. As insects become scarce as temperatures fall, a diet consisting primarily of seeds and nuts means birds need to drink more to digest their food, and in sub-zero conditions, eating snow isn’t an option for small birds because of their limited body heat.

A reliable water source also enables birds to bathe and preen, zipping individual feather barbs back together daily to maintain a waterproof insulating top layer. Vital to trap body heat on cold nights, this is also essential for efficient flight – and bare winter branches can leave birds vulnerable to predators. Keep your bird bath unfrozen and you’ll also help birds preserve energy they would otherwise waste finding an alternative water source. So, whether yours is a simple DIY bird bath you made yourself or the smartest birdie bowl money can buy, here's how to stop the water freezing over.

Seems obvious, right? But while the best place for a bird bath in summer is in partial shade to prevent algae growth, a sunnier spot in winter will help to keep a bird bath ice-free. Remember that the sunniest winter spot in your garden may be different to where the sunshine hits in summer, because the sun is lower in the sky. Think about prevailing wind direction, too, as a breeze will increase heat loss from any liquid, just as you blow on your cup of coffee to cool it down, and speed the freezing process in cold conditions.

Positioning your bird bath around 6 feet from a south-facing wall is an optimum solution. Not only will the water be warmed by sunshine for most of the day, the wall will shelter the bath from cold northerly winds and also act as a solar radiator, reflecting the sun’s heat or absorbing then releasing it once the air temperature cools. Either way, your bird bath will sit in a microclimate and the water will be slower to freeze and quicker to thaw.

Solar power is also the force behind this idea as dark stones will absorb the sun’s heat during the day, then release it as the air cools, to slow or stop bird baths freezing over. To be effective, the rock needs to be at least 4 inches across, but do match it to the size of the bird bath as it shouldn’t displace more than a third of the water. The stone should protrude above the water line as an exposed surface will heat far more quickly than a submerged one. The darker and denser the rock, the more heat it will hold, and a flattish surface will absorb more warmth.

Any object that floats on the surface of the water will constantly disrupt ice crystal formation, so it takes longer for the bird bath to freeze. Tailor your choice of what to float to how exposed your garden is, as the object needs to be light enough to move on the slightest of breezes but heavy enough to stay put in stronger winds.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In a sheltered corner, a ping pong ball is best; in a windy position, try a tennis ball. But in most gardens adding a rubber duck to your bird bath hits the sweet spot, and it doesn’t have to be yellow as this Mallard Rubber Duck from Amazon shows.

To reliably prevent ice in bird baths, use a de-icer, but be smart when shopping as many products sold as bird bath de-icers were designed for chicken coops. Look for a product with a thermostat that only works when temperatures drop and automatically shuts off once the weather warms up, so it uses minimal energy. You only need to prevent the water from freezing, not keep it warm, so a product that’s rated 60-120 watts is ideal; leave those 1000W designs for the chickens!

Another important consideration is the length of the lead, as birds often won’t use a bath positioned too close to a wall. Think about the size of your bath, too. This 9” Thermostatic Birdbath Heater from Amazon with a 5.9’ cord is great for a bigger bird bath, while this smaller 100W Bird Bath Heater, also from Amazon, with a 5’ cord would be better for an average-sized bath.

If garden aesthetics are important to you, then faux-rock designs such as this 60W Bird Bath DeIcer from Walmart bring a more natural look. You can also buy heated birdbaths with options to fit onto deck posts and balcony rails as well as ground stakes.

As temperatures drop and natural water sources freeze over, your ice-free bird bath will become a magnet for neighborhood birds. All that splashing avian action will mean you’ll need to keep the bath topped up as the bigger the volume of water, the more stable its temperature. Clear out any fallen leaves, too, as tannins will leach out and make the water unpalatable and rotting plant matter will invite unwelcome bacteria into your birdy spa.

It’s vital to scrub your bird bath once a week, particularly if neighbors don’t bother to keep their bird baths ice-free and yours becomes very busy, as that higher traffic means disease spreads more easily between birds. Use a bird-safe cleaner such as Bird Saver, available from Walmart, or a dilute solution of 10% vinegar and a scrubbing brush, and rinse well before refilling with water.

All these simple ways will keep a water supply for your garden birds, and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard through winter. So, if you're switching up your bird-feeding routine for colder weather, whether that's putting up an extra feeder, adding seasonal kitchen treats or planting shrubs laden with winter berries that birds adore, it's essential to take steps to ensure there's water alongside that welcome food.
