Some well-intentioned fall gardening chores can damage plants, weaken bulbs, harm wildlife, and rob you of next year's blooms. Here's how to avoid them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Have you ever cleaned your house so thoroughly that you tossed out important papers or other things you need? Well, the same can be true in the garden. A tidy garden isn't necessarily a healthier garden, and some common fall cleanup habits can actually compromise next year's flowers.

Yes, fall cleanup is as important as spring cleanup, but there is more room for error. At this point, plants have buds or seeds that will turn into flowers in springtime. The foliage is still storing energy to keep the plants alive through winter. Prune wrong – or make any of a dozen wrong garden moves – and you’ve set up problems for yourself and your plants.

So which autumn cleanup tasks are actually bad for your garden? I'm here to help you avoid the fall missteps that will keep you from getting a spectacular display come spring. Here are the key fall garden mistakes to watch out for – and what you should do instead.

Most spring-blooming shrubs bud on old wood. These include some of your favorite perennials, such as azaleas, lilacs, forsythia, and magnolias. If you go wild pruning in fall and chop these shrubs too, you'll cut off next spring's flower buds.

This doesn’t kill the plant, of course. The shrub will still grow healthy green leaves, but you will get very few or no blossoms when spring arrives. You’ll have to wait another 12 months to see most of those flowers.

Instead, prune spring-flowering shrubs that bloom on old wood immediately after the flowers fade. This allows them plenty of time to develop buds that will fill your garden in spring. For clean cuts on woody stems, use a sharp pair of bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8 pruning shears, which can cut branches up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick.

Summer-flowering bulbs, corms, and rhizomes use their green foliage to make food and store energy for their next flowering cycle. If you cut back the leaves of summer-flowering plants such as lilies, gladiolus, cannas, and crocosmia too early in fall, you risk depriving them of the energy they need. As a result, they may produce fewer flowers next year, or even fail to bloom altogether.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fortunately, this mistake isn't usually fatal, but it can weaken plants and affect their flowering performance. Instead, leave the foliage in place for as long as it's green and healthy, then cut it back once it naturally yellows and dies. However, frost-tender plants such as gladiolus and cannas may need to be lifted after frost damages their foliage, rather than waiting for it to die back naturally.

Tender plants such as dahlias are a little different – wait until the first frost blackens their foliage before cutting back the stems and lifting the tubers for winter storage, where necessary. Don't leave the tubers in freezing or waterlogged soil for too long, though, as they can rot.

Once lifted, store bulbs, corms, and tubers in a cool, frost-free location. Ventilated storage crates, such as these stackable, collapsible crates from CleverMade, are ideal for keeping different varieties organized while allowing air to circulate. Gladiolus corms can be stored dry after curing, while dahlias and cannas benefit from being packed in a suitable material, such as vermiculite (available on Amazon), to prevent them from drying out.

A thorough fall cleanup might leave your garden looking neat and tidy, but it can also strip away valuable food and shelter for wildlife. Many perennials produce seed heads that feed birds through the colder months, while their hollow stems and dead foliage provide overwintering habitat for beneficial insects. Cutting everything back in fall can leave these creatures with fewer places to shelter when they need them most.

Instead, leave plants such as coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, asters, and ornamental grasses standing through winter. Their seed heads provide food for finches and other backyard birds. If your garden is short on birdseed-bearing plants, you can supplement this natural food supply with a nyjer seed feeder, like this easy-clean feeder on Amazon, which is particularly attractive to goldfinches.

Standing stems can also offer nesting habitat for native bees in the following growing season. Wait until spring to tackle the cleanup, and even then, consider leaving some hollow or pithy stems standing at a height of 8–24 inches (20–60 cm). Cutting the stems creates openings that certain native bees can use for nesting, often in the following year. It's also worth leaving some fallen leaves in garden beds, as these provide overwintering shelter for butterflies, moths, and other beneficial insects. However, you should still remove diseased foliage to prevent problems from spreading next year.

Soil structure is important. If, in a flurry of fall cleaning, you dig or cultivate your garden beds too aggressively, you are actually destroying that natural soil structure. More specifically, that type of aggressive digging disrupts the habitats of beneficial earthworms and microbes. It also damages the delicate fungal networks that nurture the plant roots.

But that’s not all. When you do a lot of heavy tilling, you also run the risk of bringing up weed seeds into the upper soil, where they have a wonderful time filling your empty garden beds. Over time, repeated tilling can also break down the soil's natural structure, making it more prone to compaction, especially if you work the soil when it's wet.

Instead, choose a gentler alternative. You might layer on compost or straw right on top of the soil, allowing worms to do the work for you as they pull down food. Alternatively, install deep-rooted cover crops (like Tin Shed Seed Company's No Till Cover Crop Mix) or just loosen soil with a garden fork. Push it straight down, then just wiggle it a little.

The very word “smothering” should give you pause. If you pile on so much mulch that it smothers the plant crowns, it blocks sunlight, traps excess moisture, and keeps oxygen out of the roots. These conditions can lead to stem rot, fungal diseases, and plant death.

Instead, apply several inches of mulch (no more than 2 inches) to regulate soil temperature. Keep the mulch about 3 inches (7.5 cm) away from plant crowns. For that matter, keep it away from trunks too. A small hand rake, like this Ames one from Home Depot, makes it easy to redistribute mulch that's piled up too close to stems without disturbing the plants.

You may have heard that healthy leaf litter can decompose over time, providing nutrients for the soil. It can also shelter wildlife.

But leaving diseased foliage provides a reservoir for problems – like bacteria, pests, and fungal spores. If that happens near vulnerable plants, rain or wind can splash these pathogens onto healthy new growth. That means that the garden can be reinfected with powdery mildew and black spot.

Instead, clear fallen foliage from vulnerable plants (like roses) in fall, but dispose of it properly. Never put it in the compost; instead, bag it and put it in the garbage – these Kraft Lawn and Leaf Bags will decompose with garden waste. Then, lay down clean mulch.

With so many fall garden jobs competing for your attention, it's easy to overlook tender flowering plants that need protection before winter arrives. Dahlias, fuchsias, and tuberous begonias are all vulnerable to freezing temperatures, and forgetting about them until the first cold snap can put next year's flowers at risk.

If frost has already struck, don't panic. A little damage doesn't necessarily mean the whole plant is lost. However, the next step depends on what you're growing. Dahlias can be left until the first frost blackens their foliage, then cut back and lifted for winter storage in colder climates.

With other tender perennials, avoid rushing to prune away frost-damaged growth, as leaving it in place temporarily can offer some protection to the stems and crown. Instead, move containers somewhere sheltered or use frost cloth to protect plants from further cold. If you're using plastic covers, keep them from touching the foliage and remove them once temperatures rise to prevent overheating.

This versatile plant cover is ideally used for protecting crops from frost and pests, but can also be used for other plants.

These zip-up plant jackets protect shrubs and small trees from frost and feature drawstrings for a secure fit.

These heavy-duty planter dollies make it easy to move large pots indoors or to sheltered outdoor areas.

The best rule for fall cleanup is to keep it selective. Stripping garden beds bare is thorough – but very short sighted. So hold onto the reins before letting the autumn garden tidying run away with you.

As a final reminder, be sure to leave some seed heads and stems standing. They can make the landscape more interesting in winter, while providing food for birds and shelter for beneficial insects. It makes your garden more eco-friendly and welcoming.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7958. Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box Review 2026: Our Expert’s Opinion

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

We give the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box a rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars.

Automatic litter boxes are not just a serious time saver for cat owners; theyâre also hugely beneficial for cats, particularly those that refuse to use anything but a fresh bed of cat litter. Yet, some cat parents are hesitant about the idea of bringing home a self-cleaning litter box.

For cats accustomed to an airy, open litter tray, a compact, closed-in automatic litter box might seem like too much of a change. But itâs not always just the cat that has to be convinced. For those accustomed to the simplicity of a basic litter tray, the idea of one with a power cord and moving parts may feel a bit overwhelming.

Whether your hesitation for buying an automatic litter box comes from your fears or your catâs, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box has you covered. This unique self-cleaning litter box is designed with an open-air feel to accommodate both large and claustrophobic kitties, and its âsafe by structureâ will give nervous owners total peace of mind.

I had a chance to test the new M9 with my big kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to find out if the clever design of this litter box really makes a difference in my full Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box review below.

In my experience, there are two big reasons cat parents hesitate to make the switch from a traditional litter pan to a fancy self-cleaning litter box.

The first reason is all about the cat. Many owners fear that their cat wonât be able to adjust to the design of an automatic litter box. While traditional tray boxes are wide open on top and allow plenty of room for big cats to turn around, dig, and stand tall as they do their business, most automatic boxes are more compact.

These boxes typically have hoods or are fully enclosed. Many also have smaller litter areas, which can be difficult for larger cats to navigate.

The second issue that keeps many parents scooping manually rather than investing in a box that can do it for them is about safety.

Automatic litter boxes have a lot of moving parts. Many turn completely upside down while cleaning, so itâs natural to be worried that your cat could be frightened, pinched, or trapped by the mechanism. Of course, these boxes have

sensors and safety controls to minimize the risks of an accident, but no technology is foolproof.

With their new automatic litter box, Neakasa listened to the most common concerns of hesitant cat parents and used them to inspire their design.

For the big or claustrophobic kitty, the M9 offers a wide-open, spacious design. The bowl-shaped hood isnât as open as a traditional pan without a roof, but the tilted angle and wide mouth make it much easier for large cats to navigate. And plenty of headspace means even big kitties like Maine Coons and Ragdolls can stand up tall while they do their business.

For the claustrophobic kitty, the M9 has another trick up its sleeve: the hood and âcabinâ of the litter box are translucent. This means plenty of light gets inside, and your cat has the ability to see all around them while they assume that oh-so vulnerable position.

The Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box also has plenty of reassuring features for even the most nervous owner.

This box has many of the same safety sensors that most other automatic boxes do. These work to prevent cleaning while the cat is present and stop cleaning if your cat leaps inside mid-cycle. But what makes the M9 different is that it is structurally designed to be safe even if those sensors fail.

Thanks to the spherical design and âtilt-safeâ rotation, even if the box were to somehow enter cleaning mode while your cat was inside, they would just get a bit of a ride (like a kitty in a hamster ball). Because the M9 cabin is free of pinch points and the opening does not close or shrink during cleaning, it would be virtually impossible for a cat to be harmed.

This is exactly the kind of fail-safe design nervous cat parents need.

Founded in 2017 as Neabot, Neakasa is a smart home and pet-care technology brand headquartered in Shenzhen, China, with offices in Los Angeles and Tokyo.

Its products aim to simplify everyday cleaning and pet care. Beyond automatic litter boxes, Neakasa offers pet grooming kits with vacuum technology, smart pet water fountains, and even air-purifying litter box steps.

As you can guess, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box is a great option for larger kitties and those who arenât likely to enjoy the cramped quarters of traditional automatic litter boxes. Itâs also great for safety-conscious owners.

But plenty of other cats and cat owners are likely to find something to love about this auto litter box option.

Thanks to the extra-large 1-liter odor control system, this litter box is a great choice for owners who want premium odor control in addition to automatic cleanup. The connected phone app and weight monitoring built into the box help track litter habits in single- and multi-cat households. Plus, the relatively compact footprint makes this box a good option for smaller spaces.

The M9 includes a long list of features that make it especially cat- and owner-friendly, including:

Automatic separation of clumped waste from reusable litter

Open-view design that provides visibility of the surroundings

Spacious cabin intended to accommodate a range of cat sizes

Easily removable components for routine cleaning

Multi-cat recognition and individual habit tracking

Automatic operation according to selected settings

Continued operation using previous settings if the internet connection is interrupted

Transparent odor filter housing for visual inspection of filter condition

PureTower filter with desiccant and activated carbon that changes color when itâs time to replace

Overall dimensions: 26â long Ã 22â wide Ã 25.7â high

Waste bin capacity: 6 liters (approximately 7- to 10-day capacity for one cat)

PureTower odor-control system capacity: 1 liter.

Activated carbon and desiccant weight: 1.6 lb

Recommended clearance behind the unit: about 1.2â

Height needed for operation: about 27.2â

The Neakasa M9 works best with fast-clumping bentonite clay or mineral cat litter featuring uniform granules measuring approximately 2â4 mm. This size helps the machine sift clean litter from waste and collect clumps effectively. Crystal litter, tofu litter, and mixed litter are not recommended, as they may interfere with the automatic cleaning process.

The Neakasa M9 comes with everything needed to get started, including the litter box, a PureTower odor-control filter, a roll of 16 waste-drawer liners, five litter-emptying bags, and a power cord and adapter. It also includes a protective kitten guard, a quick-start guide, and a user manual.

Opening Size: 16.5â by 17.5â with transparent hood

Safety Features: Sensors plus tilt-safe design without pinch points or trapping potential

Odor defense: 1 liter PureTower filter with desiccant and activated carbon

Safety Features: Weight sensors, infrared sensors, and anti-pinch protection

My 12-pound Domestic Shorthair, Makoa, and I have tested a lot of automatic litter boxes in our time, and I can say with all honesty that the M9 from Neakasa is a true standout.

The litter box arrived in a rather large box with a somewhat overwhelming number of parts. But I promise you that it looks much harder than it is to put this together. Following the quick installation guide, I had it up and ready to go in less than ten minutes.

Insider tip: The installation instructions donât mention that the orange fixing ring (waste guide) at the back of the cabin must first be removed before the cabin can fit into the base.

I did have a bit of a problem getting the litter box to connect to my WiFi, which was interesting because I recently tested the Neakasa Riko Automatic Cat Feeder in the same room, using the same app, and had zero issues. But this could have just been an anomaly, because the next day I tried again and it connected right away.

Once the app was connected, everything was straightforward to set up. From there, it was hands-offâand Makoaâs time to test.

I set the M9 up in the laundry room next to his current automatic cat box, which is a more typical robot cat box with an enclosed cabin and full roof design. I know for a fact that Makoa prefers a more open design because he tends to stand up while he does his business and is a fairly large cat. Anytime he has a traditional litter pan available, he will always choose that over his current automatic litter box.

So it was no surprise to me that he immediately started using the M9 and didnât once use his old box during the testing period.

The step up into the M9 is a bit high. For smaller cats or those with mobility problems, I recommend checking out the Neakasa Air Step. I have one of these and ended up putting it in front of the M9 to catch litter, but Makoa definitely liked using it as a step as well.

In terms of odor control, cleaning prowess, and ease of use, this litter box performed exceptionally well.  As expected, the cleaning cycle stops if it senses weight or movement in the cabin, but I still really appreciate the smart design that makes it virtually impossible for a cat to get pinched or trapped if the safety sensors somehow failed and the cleaning cycle started while they were inside.

Overall, I have been really happy with this litter box, both in terms of its design and how well it cleans and reduces odors. More importantly, Makoa loves the larger space and open feel.

The 6-liter waste bin is advertised to last approximately 7â10 days for one cat, which I found to be pretty accurate. Households with multiple cats will likely need to empty it more frequently.

Yes, but for kittens under four months old, under 4.4 pounds, or shorter than 9.8 inches, the kitten guard (included) must be put in place to prevent them from getting into the waste bin area.

Yes. The PureTower system combines activated carbon and desiccant to help manage odors and moisture. Of course, regular waste removal and cleaning are still necessary for effective odor control.

If youâve been hesitant to get an automatic litter box because you think your cat might not use it because itâs too cramped, or youâre worried about safety, I highly recommend looking into the Neakasa M9.

The thoughtful design eliminates both those concerns with an open, airy cabin and a unique structural design that removes pinch points and prevents trapping. Equally important, this smart litter box features powerful odor reduction, easily removable parts for cleaning, and an effective scooping system that gives you up to 10 days of hands-off operation.

#7956. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

#7954. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! Should I Use An Allergen-Neutralizing Spray? (November 2, 2026)

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

My 1-year-old cat Daisy has allergies. She is on a special hydrolyzed diet. Iâm trying to find an allergen-neutralizing spray to cut back on dust mites in the house. Would you recommend any specific products?

Since Daisy is already on a hydrolyzed diet, it makes sense to look at environmental allergens too, especially if her allergic signs are continuing. Dust mites are common household allergens, and while the goal is to reduce the amount of allergens in her environment, eliminating them completely is not realistic. Regularly washing bedding and blankets, vacuuming with a HEPA filter, and keeping dust to a minimum are still the best places to start.

If you would like to try a spray, Purefy Anti-Allergen Spray works differently from an insecticide. It is intended to neutralize or remove the allergenic proteins associated with dust mite debris, particularly the proteins found in their feces and other microscopic particles that accumulate in household dust and fabrics. Those proteins, rather than the living mite itself, are an important source of the allergic reaction. So the idea is not to kill every mite in the house, but to reduce the allergen they leave behind.

I would specifically avoid routinely using insecticide or acaricide sprays around Daisy, even when a product is marketed as ânatural.â Cats can be particularly sensitive to certain botanical ingredients and insecticides, including some essential oils and pyrethroids. If you use an anti-allergen spray, follow the label carefully, keep Daisy away from treated surfaces until they are completely dry, ventilate the area well, and never spray it directly on her or on surfaces she is likely to lick. Please ensure you also keep it away from food and water bowls.

Think of the spray as an extra layer of environmental control, not a treatment for Daisy's allergy. The unglamorous combination of washing, HEPA vacuuming, and reducing dust is still doing most of the heavy lifting. And if Daisy continues to have significant allergic signs despite a properly conducted hydrolyzed diet trial and environmental management, it is worth investigating other possible triggers rather than simply reaching for stronger household chemicals. Usually, the answer is not a more powerful spray, but figuring out exactly what is making your cat itchy. So, real detective work is often needed for success.

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

#7953. Oh My Gourd – Understanding the Risks and Benefits of the Highly Underrated Pumpkin

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Itâs that time of year again. Before BublÃ© comes out of his cave and Mariahâs bank balance gets its annual influx, we find ourselves surrounded by candy, costumes, and a plethora of giant orange cucurbits.

Carved into ghoulish jack-oâ-lanterns for Halloween or baked into a delicious Thanksgiving pie, pumpkins have myriad uses, both decorative and delicious, and unlike many festive foods, theyâre also something our dogs can enjoy.

A member of the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae), the pumpkin is a cultivated squash, technically a fruit, with both savory and sweet culinary applications. While some countries wouldnât dare serve a roast dinner without a generous helping beside their potatoes, in the US, the nutritious pumpkin is usually relegated to seasonal decorations or the key ingredient in the eponymous pie.

There are more than 100 varieties of pumpkin with slightly different textures, flavors, and recipe applications. What they all have in common is that they are low in calories, high in antioxidants, rich in vitamins & minerals, and, when prepared correctly, safe for dogs to eat.

Compared with the potato, a vegetable commonly used in both human and canine recipes, the pumpkin is higher in fiber, much lower in carbohydrates, and is far more digestible. It is often included in diets for cats and dogs with digestive problems due to its beneficial impact on intestinal health and function.

Even the seeds of certain pumpkin varieties, when properly prepared, have been found to help eliminate intestinal parasites.1

And the cherry atop this pumpkin pie? Most dogs find the taste of pumpkin irresistible.

Though there are certainly some dogs that challenge this notion, we shouldnât use our dogs as an eco-friendly alternative waste disposal unit. While the occasional table scrap â provided the food is safe for dogs â is unlikely to cause any major catastrophes, offloading ex-display jack-oâ-lanterns and leftover pie is not a good idea.

Yes, pumpkin is a safe and healthy food we can share with dogs, but there are some dos, donâts, and precautions to be aware of.

Pumpkin is a delicious, healthy, and nutritious food that deserves to be seen as more than just a Halloween decoration or pie ingredient. Dogs love the taste, and their digestive systems will thank you.

#7951. Campbell House: A Restoration-First Renovation by Nuud Studio

From house tours and expert advice to favorite finds and DIYs.

Design-forward shops, hotels, and restaurants for your itinerary.

Renovating? Start here for expert advice, deep dives, and helpful tips.

Our catalog of more than 10,000 products featured on Remodelista.

Remodelista’s members-only directory of architects, designers, and landscape professionals.

Two years ago, we shared the sensitively renewed “bush modernist” home of architect Brad Mitchell and interior designer Kerli Valk—a thoughtful renovation that won a 2023 Australian Interior Design Awards Commendation and a 2023 Houses Award for Sustainability. Now the couple, founders of Melbourne-based Nüüd Studio, have produced another award-winning design by following the same successful formula: maximize natural light, create functional flow, focus on exquisite joinery. And, above all else, where possible, make the most of what’s already there.

“One of the most effective ways to manage a budget is to work with the existing character and materials of a building rather than trying to contradict them,” says Kerli. Here, she expounds on the idea.

“When we first saw the property, much of the interior was a combination of pine lining boards, bagged brick, and whitewashed timber ceilings. At the time it felt quite dark and dated, and understandably it was difficult for the clients to imagine how those elements could form part of a new, more contemporary interior.

“Rather than removing them, we looked at how color, texture, and light could change the way they were perceived. The existing ceilings were left largely untouched, the brick walls were celebrated rather than concealed, and the pine-clad walls were painted.

“Retaining these elements was probably one of the largest savings in the project, but it also gave the finished interior much more character. We are often more interested in transforming what is already there than replacing it. Sometimes a relatively light intervention—a change in color, texture or the way light reaches a surface—can completely alter how an existing material is experienced.”

Photography by Sean Fennessey, courtesy of Nüüd Studio.

As soon as late summer edges toward fall in New York, I begin to lick my pawpaw-loving lips. As this native North American fruit gains mainstream recognition it has become easier to source both the fresh fruit as well as pawpaw saplings. Despite the rising tide of awareness, many people are still unfamiliar with them and have yet to taste a fresh pawpaw. And if you have lusted after the perfumed fruit but have not met one, there are few things about these green-mango lookalikes you may not know.

The pawpaw under discussion is the native North American fruit belonging to the genus Asimina. The cold-hardy common pawpaw is A. triloba, but there are over a dozen other species, with regional distributions that cleave to the eastern and Mid-Western parts of the United States, from southern Canada down to Florida.

In regions and countries with Commonwealth and British colonial histories (think Australia, England, India, South Africa, the West Indies, and more) the common name “pawpaw” refers to what anyone from the Americas calls papaya. Soft-skinned and subtropical, small or football-sized, that pawpaw, Carica papaya, has yellow to deep rose flesh and is filled in the center with little black, peppery seeds. It is available in many grocery stores, year-round.

The botanical genus name Asimina is derived from the Shawnee word for pawpaw: ha’simini. For the Shawnee, September is the month of the pawpaw moon, ha’siminikiisfwa, according to Joel Barnes, Archives Director for the Shawnee Tribe (via a West Virginia Public Radio interview in a 2020).

Until the 19th century, before they were forcibly removed by the US government, the Shawnee’s ancestral lands were in pawpaw-rich Appalachia, including current southeast Ohio.

The three-day Ohio Pawpaw Festival in southeast Ohio in September is a celebration of everything pawpaw. There are pawpaw tastings, and dozens of pawpaw dishes to choose from. Chris Chmiel is one of the founders of the festival and the co-owner (with Michelle Gorman, his wife) of Integration Acres, which has sold the fresh fruit and frozen purée, and other native wild things to the public since 1996. (The first pawpaws I tasted were shipped from Ohio’s woodlands to my Brooklyn front door in 2016.)

On 18 September, 1806, William Clark wrote, in the detailed journal that Thomas Jefferson dictated the expedition keep, that “…our party entirely out of provisions Subsisting on poppaws…the party appear perfectly contented and tell us that they can live very well on the pappaws [sic].”

There are many similar entries (reading the journal is equal parts recoil and wonder; but it is a compelling chronicle of plants encountered).

The aroma of pawpaws is strong—they will perfume a room. Their texture when ripe is creamy. Different cultivars vary in flavor: Some pawpaws taste like a kaleidoscope of passionfruit and pineapple, lychee, and mango. Many tasters mention banana; personally, I detect none, but perhaps it is the pawpaw’s soft consistency that inspires the comparison. Others taste like caramel, lightly scorched. Think crème brûlée, with tropical overtones. A fruit may taste intense, or mild. The little slippery sac around each large seed is slightly bitter, as is the flesh closest to the skin.

Unless they are very close to ripe on the branch, pawpaws do not ripen well once picked (they are not like avocados). Visiting your local tree/s after a windstorm or heavy rain is a great way to find windfalls. Their skin may bruise or discolor, but this seldom means that the fruit itself is damaged. Rather, it’s a sign of ripeness.

Pawpaws are  close cousins of custard apple (cherimoya) and soursops. All these large-seeded, soft-fleshed, deeply aromatic fruit belong to the family Annonaceae. The pawpaw is the cold-hardiest among them.

There’s no reason why you would, but don’t chew up and swallow pawpaw seeds. Eating the skin has the same effect.

While the evidence is anecdotal, there is enough chatter in online forums to suggest that some people react badly to eating pawpaws. The result is dramatic diarrhea and, sometimes, nausea. Eat pawpaws in moderation (I cut myself off at three in one sitting. Is that moderate?). Also, some pawpaw purveyors, like Integration Acres, recommend against drying the pulp for use in fruit leather, since it can cause gastrointestinal distress. The reasons for this are not understood (yet).

Some researchers posit that eating pawpaws regularly could be detrimental to the eater. The seeds and pulp of pawpaws contain acetogenins, including annonacin, which is toxic to cortical neurons. Could regular pawpaw ingestion cause neurotoxins to build up over time? A connection has been drawn between pawpaws and their cousins, custard apples, which are popular in the Caribbean, where clusters of Parkinson’s in Guadalupe have been documented, possibly linked to a diet where the custard apples feature regularly. (Annonacin was also thought to play a role in cancer-cell death. That published paper has since been retracted.)

The common pawpaw is hardy from USDA growing zones 5 through 8 (according to Cornell).  It’s the tropical-tasting fruit many cool-climate gardeners can grow. Bradley Farms in New Paltz, New York (zone 5), brings pawpaws to greenmarkets in October. While pawpaws in the wild tend to grow in clonal colonies in the woods and on woodland edges, pawpaw trees will thrive in full sun as long as they have ample moisture in summer. They like hot, humid summers and cold winters.

Sowing pawpaw seed is most successful when the seeds are planted before they dry out. Even three days of drying can reduce germination rates to 20%, according to the University of Kentucky. (If you can’t plant them at once, keep them in a baggy with potting soil until you can). Sowing them in fall (right after you eat them) allows them to cold-stratify naturally, outdoors.

If you’re mosying around a pawpaw patch and are tempted to remove a sapling, think twice:  Pawpaws have long taproots and respond poorly to being yanked out.  Unless you have emerald-green thumbs, either grow them from seed or find a nursery that sells pawpaw trees. More and more do.

N.B.: This post was first published October 2023.

#7949. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

The kitchen is more than a place to cook. It’s where mornings begin, and days end—a place for conversation, sharing meals, gathering, and working. It’s one of the most lived-in rooms in the house, and the most appealing kitchens tend to feel like rooms rather than collections of equipment. The balance is in choosing appliances that can either disappear into the architecture or earn their place within it.

For more than six decades, California-founded Dacor has been considering both sides of that equation, introducing a series of innovations that have since become familiar features of the modern kitchen. Its current collection spans contemporary and transitional styles, with appliances designed to integrate into surrounding cabinetry or take a most visible role in the kitchen. Across the range, advanced features—from steam cooking and convection technology to precision refrigeration—are designed around the way a kitchen is actually used, making daily life easier rather than more complicated. Because ultimately, the best technology in the kitchen isn’t necessarily the technology you notice first; it’s what makes the room work better once you’re living in it.

November can feel like the end of things, but if you put these cottage garden and prairie favorites in the ground this month, you can enjoy beautiful early flowering displays

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November often feels like the end of the growing season in many backyards. Annual and perennial borders have likely died back for the year, and deciduous trees and shrubs stand have lost their leaves. Yet while the air is getting fresher, you can still work a little magic in your cooling soil. Because as it turns out, this month is a prime time for sowing some classic hardy flower seeds.

Many pretty cottage garden favorites, native prairie wildflowers, and pollinator staples actually need a winter chill to thrive. In nature, wild flower seeds drop from seed heads in late fall, settle into the cool earth, and take part in a natural winter cycle known as cold stratification. Exposure to freezing and thawing breaks down the tough seed jackets of key annual and perennial flower types, prompting the embryo to awaken as soon as spring conditions become favorable.

Sowing these flower seeds in November gives them a big head start. Seeds planted now establish strong roots. This means healthier conditions in spring, with sturdier stems, superior drought resistance, and prolific displays that can bloom a month ahead of spring-sown counterparts. By taking advantage of these planting conditions now, you lay the groundwork for an effortless explosion of color next season.

Keep in mind your USDA hardiness zone, your local climate, and weather conditions before deciding on specific plants and a sowing strategy. Successfully sowing flowers in November comes down to matching your plant variety with the right late-season sowing technique. There are a few primary approaches you can try with these flowers, depending on your region and weather. In mild winter climates (zones 7-10), you can try fall sowing (directly outdoors) so seeds germinate before winter, overwintering as frost-hardy rosettes that bloom in April.

In colder northern climates (zones 3-6), there is also dormant sowing. This is where seeds are sown directly into garden beds once the ground is cold enough to prevent immediate germination. Soil temperatures consistently below 45°F (7°C) allow seeds to sit dormant until early spring. For native perennial flowers or regions with erratic thaws, the best approach is winter sowing. This means sowing in outdoor containers and placing in a protected area, like an unheated cold frame, to shield seeds from rodents and heavy downpours while still providing natural chilling.

Before sowing, ground preparation is vital. Check soil temperatures before you start sowing with a good soil probe. Budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon gives a reliable read on current moisture and temperature levels. Then clear away thick, suffocating leaves, remove weeds, and lightly rake the top inch (2.5cm) of soil into a fine, crumbly tilth. Pay attention to seed packet instructions regarding sowing depth, as this can have a big effect on germination. Some larger seeds may require burying an inch deep, while fine wildflower seeds need light to germinate and need to be surface-sown with just a whisper of sand or light compost.

Water the seedbed gently with a fine mist to settle the soil without dislodging the seeds, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Mark each row clearly with durable weatherproof tags, and cover vulnerable beds with breathable floating row covers, mesh, or clean straw to deter birds. Whether sowing directly in the soil or indoors, these gorgeous flowering picks are all good to go this month…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are the quintessential cottage border bloomers. They are celebrated for their intoxicating scents and ruffled hues, which can cascade across trellises from late spring through early summer. These vintage darlings thrive in cool weather. Sowing sweet peas in November allows the seeds to develop deep roots while temperatures are low. This leads to more prolific flowering displays, with longer, sturdier stems. If you fancy a floriferous blend of lavender, violet and maroon blooms, buy Sweet Pea Burgundy Mix Sweet Peas from Eden Brothers.

In milder climates (zones 7-10), you can direct-sow sweet peas along sunny, well-draining trellises. In colder zones (3–6), sow seeds indoors in deep root-trainer tubes or biodegradable pots, and keep in an unheated greenhouse, sheltered porch, or cold frame. Sweet pea seeds have hard shells, so nick these with a nail file (or soak in room-temperature water for 12 hours prior to planting) to speed up moisture absorption. Plant seeds an inch (2.5cm) deep in rich, organic-rich soil, and pinch the central tips once seedlings develop 3 sets of true leaves for bushier plants.

With their luminous, silky petals, California poppies (Eschscholzia californica) bring effortless cheer to borders, gravel gardens, and sunny slopes. These tough-as-nails wildflowers thrive in sandy or rocky soils, making them ideal for challenging areas where other ornamentals struggle. However, because they have brittle taproots that resent disturbance, they should be direct-sown where they are intended to bloom. Buy Marde Ross & Co California Dreaming California Poppy Seed Mix from Amazon for a near-neon flush of tangerine, melon and magenta blooms.

You can sow seeds now in regions with milder winters (zones 7-10). In these areas, fall rains will trigger late-fall germination, establishing fern-like foliage that bursts into bloom by April. To sow California poppies, scatter them over the soil in an area that drains well and has full sun. Lightly rake the seeds into the soil so they are barely covered, as poppy seeds require light to germinate. If you have colder or very wet winters, it’s best to wait until spring to sow these seeds.

Offering the vertical grandeur of delphiniums without the fussy growing requirements, annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis) produces epic flowering spires in shades of royal purple, lavender, rose, and white. This cottage garden classic is a cool-season annual that is ideal for November sowing. In fact, waiting until spring often results in poor, erratic germination, as seeds need a period of stratification to break dormancy. For a shock of saturated purple-blue spires, buy QIS Dark Blue Larkspur Seeds from Eden Brothers.

Direct-sow in a rich, sunny, well-drained bed. Cover very lightly with an eighth of an inch of fine compost or sand. Winter rain and freezing nights should satisfy the seed's chilling requirements, triggering early emergence in spring. Fall-sown larkspur often blooms up to a month earlier than spring-sown seeds, beating the summer heatwaves that can cause these cool-season annuals to fade. If your winters are very cold, try winter sowing in containers.

Also known as cornflowers, bachelor’s buttons (Centaurea cyanus) are cherished vintage annuals. Their blue ruffled blooms erupt in late spring and summer to create a dazzling contrast with cottage perennials and ornamental grasses (though you can get varieties in shades of pink, purple and white). Also cold tolerant, they are naturally adapted to late-season sowing. Sowing in November helps it to grow strong roots that can withstand hotter summer days far longer than spring-started plants.

Sow in a bright, sunny border with average to poor, well-draining garden soil. Sow at roughly a quarter-inch (0.6cm) deep, firming the soil gently. For the best results, ensure the area with seeds doesn’t erode or get waterlogged over winter. In mild winter regions, seeds will sprout within a few weeks; in northern climates, they will sleep until early March, flowering from late spring all the way to July. Buy SVI Store’s Bachelor Button Mix Seeds from Amazon for a lively mixture of floral heirloom tones.

Black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) are prairie icons that light up borders from early summer well into fall. With their sunny yellow petals and chocolate-brown cones, these pollinator-friendly perennials and biennials are often bought as transplants. Hardy in zones 3-9, they are super tough. However, their seeds possess dormancy inhibitors that can lead to patchy germination in spring soil. November sowing solves this problem naturally. By scattering now, you allow the rhythm of winter rains, snow cover, and sub-freezing nights to break dormancy smoothly.

Clear away heavy mulch and scatter seeds thinly over the surface. They require light to germinate, so press them into the soil without burying them. While fall-sown plants spend their first spring developing roots and crowns, many will reward you with late-summer blooms in the first year. Buy Harris Seeds’ Rudbeckia Goldilocks Seeds from Walmart for a ruffled twist on the dazzling classic. Just keep in mind that many varieties benefit from cold exposure, but not all, so know your type before you sow.

With their delicate, two-toned blooms and graceful spurs, columbines (Aquilegia spp.) bring woodland romance and grace to borders, cottage beds, and rockeries. Native across North America and Europe, Aquilegia species are hardy down to zone 3. Seeds require 4-6 weeks of cold, damp stratification, making November sowing the easiest, most reliable way to propagate them. Buy Blue Star Columbine Seeds from Eden Brothers for a vivid bounty of iconic violet-blue and white blooms.

Select a site that receives gentle morning sun and dappled afternoon shade with rich, well-draining soil. Some varieties require sunlight to trigger germination, so check the seed packet. Scatter seeds onto the soil surface and press lightly into the earth, but don’t cover with soil. If you live in an area with winter gales or heavy rains, you can winter-sow columbines into ventilated plastic jugs in a shaded outdoor spot. Seedlings will emerge in spring, providing pretty nectar for returning hummingbirds.

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a perennial staple in the sustainable, pollinator-friendly yard. Featuring daisy-like blooms and spiky cones, echinacea feeds native bees and butterflies in summer, while offering seed cones for goldfinches in fall. Seeds have evolved to weather harsh winters before germinating, making November a great time for sowing. Buy Purple Coneflower Heirloom Seeds by the Kviter Store from Amazon for a generous supply of purple drifts.

Broadcast seeds in a sunny spot with well-drained, average soil. Echinacea seeds need minimal light filtering through to sprout, so rake them into the earth no more than an eighth of an inch deep, firming the soil. Winter's freeze-thaw cycles settle the seeds, softening their husks so that strong roots push down early in spring. While coneflowers focus heavily on root establishment in the first year, November-sown echinacea tend to bloom reliably by the second season.

Your gardening season doesn’t have to be over in November. Taking a little time this month to start off some pretty cottage garden and pollinator favorites is such a rewarding investment in future backyard bloomers. By partnering with winter’s cold cycles rather than fighting them, you give these key annuals and perennials a real head start on early spring beauty. Using seeds is also a cost-effective way to get more flowers. If some don’t germinate or establish, you haven’t lost a lot of money. So grab a few seed packets, prep your beds, and get planting. It’s time to start looking forward to an effortless run of blooms well ahead of the neighbors.

#7946. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! What Happens If Cherry Eye Is Left Untreated? (November 2, 2026)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an issue for me right now.â

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is important to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Talk to your vet about a payment plan, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most important first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

#7943. Drought-Tolerant Perennials for Mid-Atlantic Gardens

When we think of drought-tolerant plants, we often picture prairie plants with deep roots that can reach far into the soil for moisture. But after years of gardening in the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic, I’ve learned that deep roots aren’t the only reason a plant can withstand dry conditions. Some of the most resilient plants have surprisingly shallow root systems.

The following three perennials have impressed me with their ability to handle drought once established. Two are excellent choices for sunny gardens, while the third proves that even difficult, dry shade can support beautiful plants.

Read More: Best Plants for Your Shopping List in the Mid-Atlantic

Size: 12 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide

Conditions: Full sun; dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil

Butterfly weed is one of those plants that I wish more gardeners would grow. With all the encouragement to plant milkweed for monarch butterflies, many people immediately think of common milkweed. But common milkweed can spread vigorously through rhizomes and seed, sometimes crowding out neighboring plants. Butterfly weed offers a much more compact alternative, with a wonderful mounding habit and gorgeous bright orange flowers.

I love orange in the garden and use it extensively, particularly alongside white flowers. But if orange isn’t your favorite color, there are yellow-flowered selections of butterfly weed, too. I recently visited a friend’s gravel garden in Wilmington, Delaware, where orange and yellow plants were growing together and producing seedlings with different flower colors.

As a prairie plant, butterfly weed needs excellent drainage. Its long, tuberous roots help it withstand dry conditions once established, but those roots also mean it’s best to choose a permanent location rather than move mature plants around the garden. Be patient during establishment. Butterfly weed may take a little time to get going, but it can live for many years. And beyond its value to pollinators, I think it’s every bit as pretty as the more traditional ornamental perennials we grow.

Conditions: Full sun; dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil

If you asked me to name my favorite perennials, lesser calamint would probably make my top five. I spent about 25 years gardening in the Madison, Wisconsin, area, where I was fortunate to be surrounded by some remarkable horticulturists. Roy Diblik was among those who introduced many of us to this plant through his work at Northwind Perennial Farm. Once we saw how well it performed, we started growing it ourselves.

Lesser calamint produces masses of tiny white flowers that remind me of baby’s breath. It has a lovely, rounded habit, and that fine texture is especially effective when mixed with larger-leaved or coarser plants. There are selections with pale blue or lavender flowers, but I’m perfectly happy with the bright white blooms. When the plant is in full flower, it can be absolutely covered with pollinating insects.

And this is one tough perennial. I’ve seen lesser calamint used in difficult roadside plantings where it performed exceptionally. The important thing is to keep excess moisture away from its roots. Give it plenty of sunlight and well-drained soil, and it can handle dry conditions remarkably well.

Gardeners sometimes worry about plants that seed around, but I’ve never found lesser calamint particularly troublesome. It may produce a few seedlings, but they’re easy to recognize and remove. It’s a reliable, good-looking plant that plays well with others.

Size: 9 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide

Conditions: Partial to full shade; well-drained soil; tolerates dry shade once established

Epimedium is one of my favorite examples of why we shouldn’t assume that drought-tolerant plants need deep roots. Its roots are shallow and fibrous, forming a relatively flat mat that’s easy to lift when dividing plants. Looking at that root system, you might expect epimedium to be one of the first plants to suffer during a drought. But I’ve seen exactly the opposite.

Several years ago, I attended an American Public Gardens Association conference in Toronto during a severe drought. We visited a garden where the perennial borders were suffering terribly. Nearly everything had wilted from the lack of moisture, yet the epimedium foliage looked as though it had been watered all along. That experience has stayed with me.

Not every epimedium is equally drought tolerant, but many selections perform wonderfully in dry shade once established. They’re especially useful as ground covers beneath trees and in woodland gardens.

One of my favorites to recommend is ‘Lilafee’ (Epimedium grandiflorum ‘Lilafee’), a vigorous selection with lovely purple flowers. Epimedium flowers are delicate, almost like little fairies hovering above the foliage. They’re the sort of flowers that make you stop, kneel down, and look closely. I think we need more plants that encourage us to slow down and enjoy our gardens.

Epimediums can be expensive, particularly when you’re trying to establish a large planting. My advice is to buy a couple each year rather than waiting until you can afford a dozen. Over time, those few plants can develop into a beautiful planting, and you’ll be glad you started.

To learn more about these plants from Ed, as well as five more drought-tolerant plant recommendations, check out our podcast: Episode 4: Plants for Drought.

#7942. Renovation Diaries: The House Envelope and Other Lessons in Efficiency

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Editor’s note: This is the latest in a series of posts by Sally Kohn— journalist and CNN political commentator, TED talk giver, and design aficionado—chronicling her adventures in remodeling.

Let’s level set. I live in a 1780s barn that was turned into a house in the 1950s, and as far as I can tell the windows and the siding haven’t been changed since. The fact is, many parts of our money pit farmhouse need updating. Some, like the 1950s asphalt roof built directly on top of a much older shake shingle roof, we replaced last year. Other things we’re still waiting on, like the vintage 1950s bathroom tile with vintage crumbling grout. But since we can’t close many of our windows without pushing on them from the outside, and we have an inexplicable leak behind our very ancient siding, we put off the inevitable long enough. It is time for some grand-scale renovations.

Stay tuned for some of the other things we’ll be changing, including a kitchen refresh. But first up, if we’re going to go to all the trouble—and, ahem, expense—of replacing all of our siding and windows, can we make our old home more environmentally responsible in terms of both materials and energy efficiency? Let’s find out.

My guide on this journey is Shannon Pendleton, principal of Sanderson Sustainable Design and co-host of Passive House Accelerator. In addition to being a friend and neighbor, Shannon is a leading expert on how to make homes more sustainable and energy efficient. And while those concepts might immediately make you think of solar panels and the like, Shannon explains that in energy efficiency, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. In other words, using green energy to power your home is great. But designing your home to need less energy in the first place is even better.

But with apologies to Shannon, when she explained the science of the “building envelope,” all I could think about is that envelope feels like the wrong word. Maybe it should be “building envelop”—as in, how enveloped is your building. Because your “building envelop” is what stops the outside environment from getting in and the inside environment from getting out. That means everything from bugs and dust to wind to heat and cold.

So I’m making two big changes to my “building envelop,” both of which create an opportunity for more energy efficiency. Let’s start with the siding. We have very old, very stained, very falling-apart cedar. I could just replace it with cedar, maybe even sustainably harvested cedar. But the fact is, our old cedar is cupping and splitting. Yes, more maintenance would help, but that’s hard to do with second-story wood. Also I’m lazy. Alternatively, I could have gone with some plastic product or chemically treated wood but, like I said, we care about the environment and also want to preserve the look and feel of our historic home. So we’re going with Thermory siding.

Thermory takes sustainably forested wood—in our case, we’re using pine—and puts it through an intense heat-treating process that makes the wood more stable and rot-resistant. It’s an updated twist on the Japanese shou sugi ban process, where wood is charred to make it water and rot resistant. Thermory is that, without the blackening (though they actually do have a product that mirrors the shou sugi ban look, but with the added benefits of Thermory’s advanced thermal modification). In other words, Thermory gives us everything we like about natural wood plus all these added benefits.

Using a more stable rot-resistant siding definitely envelops our house better (take that, flying squirrels), but the energy efficiency upgrades come from what will be behind the siding. Our contractor—the wonderful, lovable, fantastic-to-work-with John Gemmi and his company, Gemmi Construction—were already planning to weather-seal behind the siding, and of course put new insulation behind that where we find any lacking. But Shannon suggested installing “a rain screen, a continuous air barrier, and continuous exterior insulation” to give us the most enveloped envelope possible. Ultimately, we settled on Zip R sheathing, which does all three of those things in one system. So that’s our plan.

As for the windows, well…. The most energy-efficient option is triple-pane glass, but in our case, since we’re replacing a gajillion windows, we just couldn’t make it work in our budget. We have two walls of windows in our great room, most of which are currently fixed panes that we’re excited to replace with operable awning windows. We looked into doing triple-pane for just those windows, but that would have made the windows too heavy to open. So yes, we’re choosing a little less efficiency there but counting on the fact that having new windows that don’t require a screwdriver and grunts to close will nevertheless up our efficiency. Plus, thanks to Ambiance Design, we’re adding retractable Duette Honeycomb shades over those large window walls, which will give us some extra energy efficiency on super hot days.

Niece Lumber helped us pick out Lincoln Windows, a family run U.S.-manufactured brand with two advantages. First, we could get retractable screens which we’re very excited about. And second, they offer custom colors on their exteriors. You’ll have to stay tuned to figure out what color choice we’ve made. It’s gonna be…dramatic.

Work on the siding and window part of the renovation is starting soon. I’ll be posting updates on my Instagram (@sallykohn), plus more updates along the way here as we get into our kitchen renovations, including the most sustainable and cool countertop and our very locally made and custom color stove. Watch this space!
