Trying to make compost from fallen leaves takes forever, right? Not if you know this gardeners’ trick to get it ready to use in your yard in time for spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Making free compost from fall leaves is such an easy win, and with these smart hacks you’ll have a nutritious mix ready to enrich your garden soil by spring. While creating traditional leaf mold compost can take up to two years, this quick and easy method speeds up decomposition to bring garden-ready compost in 4-5 months. What’s more, it’s mess-free!

Want to know the secret? Any compost pile relies on tiny organisms, way too small for us to see without a microscope, to break plant matter down. These microbes are responsible for around 80-90% of the chemical decomposition process when making compost, and this method simply creates the ideal conditions for the speediest members of this recycling workforce to flourish.

It’s cheap, too, as you’re going to make compost in a black trash bag. Heavy-duty contractor bags such as Brute Super Tuff Bags, available from Walmart, are best as they’re much stronger than those designed for residential use. Your reward will be a rich and crumbly, well-structured compost that will feed plants as well as help soil hold moisture. Spread it as a mulch onto perennial borders and around shrubs to lock moisture in and deliver nutrients to roots. Dig it into veggie beds to fuel healthy crops, or mix with coco coir to make your own potting mix. You can even steep a scoop in a bucket of water for a couple of days to make a compost tea that’ll help protect your plants from disease.

Ready? Part of the Weekend Wins series, making a quick compost from fall leaves is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward. Here's what to do.

Not all leaves break down at the same speed, and many species have evolved strong defences against microbes. Oak, beech, sycamore, horse chestnut, holly, laurel and magnolia leaves are all high in a compound called lignin that acts as a protective armor against microbes. They’re also rich in tannins, a compound that effectively halts the digestive action of microbes, so they're slow to decompose.

Instead, use foliage that’s thin, flexible and soft to make compost from autumn leaves. Maple, ash, elderberry, willow and fruit tree foliage are all far lower in lignin and tannin so they’ll break down in a fraction of the time. It doesn't matter if a few high-lignin, high-tannin leaves get mixed in, but keep them to a minimum. And don't worry if you're not sure about tree identification: just avoid using thick, leathery or glossy leaves.

Cutting the leaves up into smaller sections also speeds up the process by increasing the surface area and exposing the less protected innards of the foliage for the microbial feasting. Shredding leaves before composting is the equivalent of chopping a log into kindling: you give the microbes plenty of vulnerable material that quickly gets the process going.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The chopped-up material won’t mat together like whole leaves do, and it'll absorb water rather than repelling it, both also speeding decomposition.

Shredding leaves is easy to do, even if you don’t have a leaf shredder. Simply run your lawnmower over the leaves multiple times or tip the foliage into an old trash can and shred with a string trimmer or weed whacker.

In any compost pile you need to mix carbon – the ‘browns’ – with nitrogen – the ‘greens’ – for microbes to work efficiently. And this applies when you make compost from fall leaves, too. Leaves are very high in carbon so, to get a good balance of browns and greens to keep those microbes happy, you need to add some nitrogen.

Grass clippings are super-high in nitrogen: use a lawnmower to shred leaves on your lawn and the job’s done for you. Coffee grounds are also nitrogen-rich so toss those in, and if you have access to free chicken manure, that works a treat, too. Aim for one part greens to three parts brown.

To kickstart the decomposition process, toss a shovelful or two of garden soil – or homemade compost if you have it – into the mix. This will be packed full of microbes that will immediately get to work.

Microbes work best in damp conditions so pour water over the leaf mix, unless of course it's recently rained and the leaves are already wet. Aim for moist not wet, as you don’t want the leaves sitting in water.

Making compost this way requires oxygen so when you tie the sack closed (using a zip tie is easiest) don’t squash all the air out of the sack first. So this air can be replaced, delivering a fresh supply of oxygen, use a sharp knife to punch air holes into the sack. Around 15 holes in a regular contractor sack is about right, and try to distribute them well around the sides and base of the sack.

Those microbes are going to generate plenty of heat as they get to work, and you can help retain that warmth by storing the bag in a sunny, sheltered spot so the black plastic absorbs lots of solar heat. Tucking the bag against a south-facing wall or shed-side is ideal as here it'll enjoy plenty of sunshine and be shielded from cold northerly winds.

When you make traditional leaf mold compost, you rely on the battalion of slow-working fungi among the microbial army to do the hard work. But in this accelerated composting method, you want to encourage the fast-working bacteria contingent to head up the recycling force. To do this, you need to regularly aerate the compost and add fresh oxygen, and the easiest way to do this is to give the bag a shake, flip it over or simply kick it along the ground every few days.

Do all these steps and your homemade compost will be ready to use in 4-5 months, right on time for when your garden wakes up in spring. You’ll know when it’s ready, even without opening the bag. While the microbes are busy breaking down the leaf mix, the contents will feel warmer to the touch; once they’re done, the temperature of the bag with match the ambient air temperature.

When you do open the bag, the compost should smell earthy, like a fresh forest floor. If you notice a slightly sour note, simply leave the sack open for a week or so to allow the compost to air.

Then you’re all ready to use your free compost to give your garden plants a nutritious boost for healthy growth, abundant blooms and bumper crops. Making a quick compost is one of the best ways to use fallen leaves in your garden so put this easy task on your list of garden jobs to do in fall.

This feature is part of the Weekend Wins series, packed with quick and easy gardening tasks that bring a big reward.

Waterlogged soil is the prime reason potted plants fail in fall and winter, and this speedy solution couldn't be simpler.

This great-value gardening tool transforms lawns in fall, fast, if you want lush grass next year for next-to-no effort.

Christmas cactus blooms are a delightful part of holiday decor when you trick plants into flowering on time.

Tuck cold-hardy pansies into pots and hanging baskets for months of easy-breezy fall-to-winter blooms.

Plant fast-growing bulbs in your lawn and enjoy drifts of lavender-hued blooms in a few weeks.

Remove suckers that are stealing energy from your rose shrubs and enjoy bigger blooms next summer.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#7939. Off Hours: How Landscape Design Star Cleve West Survives His Day Job

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

What does a top garden designer do to relax? He gardens, of course—but not exactly where you’d expect. Cleve West, winner of seven Chelsea Flower Show RHS Gold Medals, spends his free time tending to a plot that couldn’t be more different from the conceptual spaces he creates for clients. Not especially private and the opposite of chic, his patch is in a West London community garden (in the UK it is called an allotment) and has been his personal project for a decade.

Cleve’s 2011 book, Our Plot, part memoir, part manual, part state-of-the-world discourse, takes us through the highs and lows of allotment life. Meanwhile, we’ve been invited for lunch:

Cleve West is the Gary Cooper of the garden design world. Modest, sincere, assured, he is admired by all. Did I mention that he can cook? Besides growing vegetables, fruit, and flowers, Cleve does a surprising amount of entertaining in the allotment that he shares with his partner, Christine Eatwell.

They use a variety of garden-side cooking contraptions: a grill, a gas-fired oven, and a hand-built pizza oven. “Many hours are spent not growing vegetables,” admits Cleve, shown here with his grill, picked up in Normandy, and the impressive pizza oven, which has a brick base, mud and sawdust dome, and bottles placed in the middle to stop the heat from going down.

“Some people think that the word ‘design’ is a little too pretentious and would rather their garden ‘evolve’ over the years,” says Cleve. “But how you arrange your plot, whether you draw it on paper or not, is design.” His intriguing wild tangle—I mean design—contains a rotation of vegetables including squash, beans, leaks, artichoke, onions, and gladioli by the shed.

Cleve’s client-based designs are characterized by sculptural forms and so, too, is his allotment. Wigwams made from coppiced hazel are finished off with heavy duty chains instead of insubstantial twine. They support beans and gourds, and last for about a season.

Recycle, improvise, and modify. This is the heart of the British community garden ethos. “If I had control over all the allotments, I would ban pre-fabricated sheds,” says Cleve. “I’d urge people to make their own in the name of local distinctiveness and individuality.”

Cooking at the plot intensifies the enjoyment of fresh food. Basic ingredients—seasoning, spices, oil, and vinegar—are kept in one of the sheds, but key elements, such as pizza dough, are made at home and carried in. True, cooking and entertaining without electricity and hot water involves extra work, but chopping and frying onions is far preferable out of doors than in.

Feeling inspired? Here’s Cleve’s recipe for a simple relish made on a barbecue or makeshift grill. He promises that allotment cooking “doesn’t get much easier.” Pair with naan or pita bread for a quick lunch.

Put the eggplant and green tomatoes on the barbecue or open fire and char them until they are black and “all squidgy” inside. Then cut along the middle and scoop out the contents of both eggplants and tomatoes. Mash, add the rest of the ingredients, mix, and eat!

N.B.: This post was first published July 2013. It has been updated with new links and information. For an update on Cleve’s allotment, read his recent blog post.

#7938. Late Summer Through Fall in Susan’s Minnesota Garden, Part 1

Hi GPODers! Today we’re welcoming back longtime contributor Susan from St. Paul, Minnesota (Zone 5a). Susan has shared her garden with us many times over the years, and today she’s taking us through some of her favorite moments from late July into October. If you’ve missed her previous visits, you can revisit last year’s gardening season at the 45th parallel. For now, let’s see what she’s been growing!

Still looking back: Here are some photos from late July to October.

Back garden, late July: I had a huge ‘Montana Aureomarginata’ hosta (Hosta montana ‘Aureomarginata’, Zones 3–8) in the front garden, where it received too much sun. My husband dug it up for me, and I divided it into three clumps, one of which is pictured above. The bluish hostas are ‘El Niño’ (Hosta ‘El Niño’, Zones 3–9), and the hydrangea is ‘Little Quick Fire’ panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘SMHPLQF’, Zones 3–8).

A second clump of ‘Montana Aureomarginata’ was replanted in the front garden, but in a shady spot under a white cedar (Thuja occidentalis, Zones 2–7).

Speaking of hostas, this is one of my favorites; even the almost pinkish flowers are pretty. The similarly colored companion is Chinese astilbe (Astilbe chinensis, Zones 4–8).

Grape-leaf anemone (Anemone tomentosa ‘Robustissima’, Zones 4–8) glows in the late-afternoon sun.

Front garden with end-of-summer gold and fuchsia: Garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia cvs., Zones 3–9), and a daylily blossom (Hemerocallis ‘Autumn Gold’, Zones 3–9; Sutton, 1952, not the more recent one) missed by the deer.

I was doing some planting in a redone, seldom-visited corner of the garden when I thought I spotted a piece of trash. It turned out to be a lone stalk and blossom of Japanese lily (Lilium speciosum ‘Album’, Zones 5–8) that had somehow escaped the scarlet lily beetle ravages and that I, too, had missed in my cutting-down frenzy. I have hope that the others will have survived.

According to Old House Gardens, this is a wild ancestor of ‘Casa Blanca’. OHG last offered it in 2012, and it is now considered “commercially extinct in the Netherlands.”

The painted lady butterflies love curly onion (Allium senescens ‘Glaucum’, Zones 4–8) as much as I do. Its long-lasting blooms perk up the late-summer, early-fall garden.

‘Autumn Joy’ stonecrop (Hylotelephium ‘Herbstfreude’, Zones 3–9) is a dependable fall bloomer, beloved by pollinators.

Another fall bloomer that attracts many pollinators is black cohosh, also known as bugbane (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8). This photo was taken on September 22, but other clumps of it are still blooming more than a month later.

‘Sun King’ Japanese spikenard (Aralia cordata ‘Sun King’, Zones 3–9) is prized for its golden foliage, but it also develops small but interesting flowers and fruits late in the season.

Thank you for sharing another look at your garden with us, Susan! I especially loved the surprise lily. Finding a flower you thought you’d lost is always exciting, especially after dealing with pests!

We have more photos from Susan to share soon, so stay tuned for Part 2!

If you're thinking of cleaning your deck with vinegar, take care not to make this mistake...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Somewhere in the pantry there's probably a gallon of white vinegar that already cleans the coffee pot and the shower door. Vinegar costs next to nothing and smells like salad dressing instead of bleach; many people use vinegar to clean a deck for exactly those reasons, without a second thought about where the rinse water goes.

Out in the yard, white vinegar already has a few honest jobs. Some gardeners use vinegar in the garden to scrub crusty clay pots and burn back weeds in sidewalk cracks. That same weed-killing action is part of the problem on a deck, though. Acetic acid burns plant tissue on contact, and a bucket of rinse water doesn't stop at the edge of the boards.

It also matters what the deck is made of. A cedar deck that has never seen a drop of stain, for example? Well, that doesn't play by the same rules as Trex, a major composite brand that actually approves vinegar for one particular job. Check the maker's care guide before any cleaner goes on.

On some composite boards, the answer is a qualified yes. If your boards are one of Trex's current lines, white vinegar is on the approved list for hard water deposits: the chalky white spots a sprinkler leaves when it keeps hitting the same boards.

Rinse well afterward; everyday dirt gets warm soapy water and a soft-bristle brush instead, scrubbed down into the embossed grain. Be aware that Trex says anything containing acid or bleach can lighten the color of its boards, so try a small spot near the steps first.

Other brands say less. TimberTech's care guide doesn't mention vinegar at all, and it points owners toward its own diluted deck cleaner or, for railings, a pH-neutral detergent. It also warns against citrus cleaners, solvents and several brand-name deck cleaners on its current capped boards. When a manufacturer hasn't approved a product, using it anyway means guessing how the surface will react.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Wood decks raise a different question, and the finish on top matters more than the boards underneath. Acids aren't foreign to deck care – oxalic acid brighteners are a standard step for pulling gray discoloration out of bare wood before a fresh coat of stain.

That's prep work for unfinished boards, though; once paint or stain goes on, the can it came in has the final word. Some finish makers approve only their own cleaners, and washing a stained deck with straight vinegar again and again means working outside those directions with no way of knowing how that particular finish will hold up.

Then there's everything growing below the deck rail. Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid, the same acid sold in stronger form as a weed killer, and it damages leaf tissue wherever it lands.

Picture that rinse water running off the edge of the deck onto a bed of hostas or a row of fall lettuce – leaves that it soaks can turn brown and crispy, and seedlings take the worst of it. The acid doesn't hang around in the soil, and lawn grass along the edge usually recovers better than broadleaf plants do. A natural label? It sadly doesn't change any of that.

The broom comes out first, since scrubbing wet leaves only smears them across the boards. Home Depot's 7-pattern Ames hose nozzle set has a soft shower setting for soaking the deck and a narrow jet for packed gaps. Warm water and a squirt of dish soap handle ordinary grime on wood and composite alike.

Brushes are where the two big composite brands part ways. Trex wants soft bristles, and Home Depot also carries a soft-bristle Unger scrub brush that threads onto a standard broom handle. TimberTech calls for medium-to-stiff nylon on its composite instead. Do one section at a time and rinse it before the suds dry.

Mildew and gray weathering on a wood deck usually need something stronger than soap. Walmart carries DEFY's powdered wood cleaner, an oxygen-based formula for exterior wood that mixes up in a bucket.

Now, at least one stain maker warns that chlorine bleach can damage both the finish and the bare wood fibers, and it's hard on any plants it splashes. Capped composite needs more caution here (TimberTech's guide says its own diluted cleaner is the safe bet). Think about where the bucket water goes, too, especially if the deck slopes toward a fish pond or a storm drain. A label that says biodegradable means the product breaks down eventually, not that it's harmless to fish and other pond life along the way.

Pressure washers are tempting on a big deck, but a narrow stream held too close can tear up the surface of wood boards and leave the fibers fuzzy. Composite brands set firm limits. On Trex Transcend, Enhance and Select boards, the limit is 3,100 psi with a fan tip held at least 8 inches (20.3cm) from the surface, though the company doesn't recommend pressure washers at all on its early-generation lines. TimberTech caps pressure at 1,500 psi, for rinsing only, with the spray running along the grain.

Decks that get washed twice a year are far less likely to need anything harsh. Trex ties its spring and fall schedule to pollen and leaf litter, since that buildup is what mold grows on. Leaves wedged between boards can hold water against the surface long after a rain, and a putty knife slid down the row clears them out quickly. Shady corners and boards under overhanging branches usually go green first.

Keep the vinegar, just not as the everyday deck cleaner. On Trex boards with chalky sprinkler spots, it's the fix the company itself approves, and the potting bench can use it too. Day-to-day grime comes off with warm soapy water and a brush that won't scuff the boards, ideally on a gray afternoon when the sun isn't drying the suds faster than you can scrub.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

Editor’s note: This is the latest in a series of posts by Sally Kohn— journalist and CNN political commentator, TED talk giver, and design aficionado—chronicling her adventures in remodeling.

Let’s level set. I live in a 1780s barn that was turned into a house in the 1950s, and as far as I can tell the windows and the siding haven’t been changed since. The fact is, many parts of our money pit farmhouse need updating. Some, like the 1950s asphalt roof built directly on top of a much older shake shingle roof, we replaced last year. Other things we’re still waiting on, like the vintage 1950s bathroom tile with vintage crumbling grout. But since we can’t close many of our windows without pushing on them from the outside, and we have an inexplicable leak behind our very ancient siding, we put off the inevitable long enough. It is time for some grand-scale renovations.

Stay tuned for some of the other things we’ll be changing, including a kitchen refresh. But first up, if we’re going to go to all the trouble—and, ahem, expense—of replacing all of our siding and windows, can we make our old home more environmentally responsible in terms of both materials and energy efficiency? Let’s find out.

My guide on this journey is Shannon Pendleton, principal of Sanderson Sustainable Design and co-host of Passive House Accelerator. In addition to being a friend and neighbor, Shannon is a leading expert on how to make homes more sustainable and energy efficient. And while those concepts might immediately make you think of solar panels and the like, Shannon explains that in energy efficiency, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. In other words, using green energy to power your home is great. But designing your home to need less energy in the first place is even better.

But with apologies to Shannon, when she explained the science of the “building envelope”, all I could think about is that envelope feels like the wrong word. Maybe it should be “building envelop”—as in, how enveloped is your building. Because your “building envelop” is what stops the outside environment from getting in and the inside environment from getting out. That means everything from bugs and dust to wind to heat and cold.

So I’m making two big changes to my “building envelop”, both of which create an opportunity for more energy efficiency. Let’s start with the siding. We have very old, very stained, very falling-apart cedar. I could just replace it with cedar, maybe even sustainably harvested cedar. But the fact is, our old cedar is cupping and splitting. Yes, more maintenance would help, but that’s hard to do with second-story wood. Also I’m lazy. Alternatively, I could have gone with some plastic product or chemically treated wood but, like I said, we care about the environment and also want to preserve the look and feel of our historic home. So we’re going with Thermory siding.

Thermory takes sustainably forested wood—in our case, we’re using pine—and puts it through an intense heat-treating process that makes the wood more stable and rot-resistant. It’s an updated twist on the Japanese shou sugi ban process, where wood is charred to make it water and rot resistant. Thermory is that, without the blackening (though they actually do have a product that mirrors the shou sugi ban look, but with the added benefits of Thermory’s advanced thermal modification). In other words, Thermory gives us everything we like about natural wood plus all these added benefits.

Using a more stable rot-resistant siding definitely envelops our house better (take that, flying squirrels), but the energy efficiency upgrades come from what will be behind the siding. Our contractor—the wonderful, lovable, fantastic-to-work-with John Gemmi and his company, Gemmi Construction—were already planning to weather-seal behind the siding, and of course put new insulation behind that where we find any lacking. But Shannon suggested installing “a rain screen, a continuous air barrier, and continuous exterior insulation” to give us the most enveloped envelope possible. Ultimately, we settled on Zip R sheathing, which does all three of those things in one system. So that’s our plan.

As for the windows, well….The most energy-efficient option is triple-pane glass, but in our case, since we’re replacing a gajillion windows, we just couldn’t make it work in our budget. We have two walls of windows in our great room, most of which are currently fixed panes that we’re excited to replace with operable awning windows. We looked into doing triple-pane for just those windows, but that would have made the windows too heavy to open. So yes, we’re choosing a little less efficiency there but counting on the fact that having new windows that don’t require a screwdriver and grunts to close will nevertheless up our efficiency. Plus, thanks to Ambiance Design, we’re adding retractable Duette Honeycomb shades over those large window walls, which will give us some extra energy efficiency on super hot days.

Niece Lumber helped us pick out Lincoln Windows, a family run U.S.-manufactured brand with two advantages. First, we could get retractable screens which we’re very excited about. And second, they offer custom colors on their exteriors. You’ll have to stay tuned to figure out what color choice we’ve made. It’s gonna be…dramatic.

Work on the siding and window part of the renovation is starting soon. I’ll be posting updates on my Instagram (@sallykohn), plus more updates along the way here as we get into our kitchen renovations, including the most sustainable and cool countertop and our very locally made and custom color stove. Watch this space!

#7932. Frostweed: A Drought-Tolerant Native with a Twist

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Learn more about frostweed, one of Amy Galloway Medley’s favorite underappreciated native plants to grow.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

I believe there are misconceptions about this plant because of the word “weed” in its name. Some people might see frostweed as a woodland plant that should stay in the wild and does not belong in cultivated gardens, but I wholeheartedly disagree. It grows about 6 feet tall, making it a good choice for the back of a border, but you can also control the stature by cutting it back in spring.

Along with the height it can bring to your designs, frostweed produces clusters of gorgeous white blooms from late summer through fall. It also has large, interesting leaves, and the stems have winglike flanges that run down their length. These sturdy stems put on another show after a frost.

The plant gets its name because a hard freeze will sometimes make the stems split, causing the moisture inside to erupt out in sheets of ice that look like cotton candy. I’ve heard that a cutback just before the first hard freeze will cause ice spirals to come out of the tops of the stems, but I have not yet managed to get the timing right on my plants.

In the wild, you’ll find frostweed underneath big shade trees, and it is highly drought tolerant. In a cultivated garden with supplemental water, it can also grow in full sun, making it adaptable to a range of conditions. Frostweed’s most valuable characteristic, however, is its benefit to pollinators and wildlife. When planted in sun, it quickly attracts an array of pollinators. The winged stems are also perfect for certain species of bees and other stem-nesting insects. Leave it standing in winter and birds will feast on its seeds.

Learn more from Amy about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Amy Galloway Medley is the lead horticulturist at Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

There was a time when any tree injury had us reaching for cans of black tar and wound dressings, but is sealing really a good idea? Here’s the truth about what your trees need

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some garden wisdom isn’t really wise at all. Have you ever heard that sprinkling used coffee grounds around hydrangeas adds oodles of acid to the soil, or that peony buds won’t open unless ants tickle their petals? Far from being wisdoms, these are classic examples of garden folklore: ideas that have been repeated so often across fences and forums that people simply assume they are true.

Welcome back to Garden Mythbusters, where we aim to separate fact from fiction with persistent gardening beliefs. We have already examined whether gravel at the bottom of pots truly helps drainage and the idea that bulbs need to be planted pointy side up. Here’s another one that you might not even have suspected was a myth: the idea that when you sever a branch or clean up storm damage, you must slather the fresh wood with pruning paint or tar sealant to prevent rot, pests, and disease.

For generations, we’ve been encouraged to buy sealants and dressings to protect our damaged trees. Watching an oak or maple bleed sap feels alarming, and reaching for a sealant seems like a responsible way to shield against infection. But should you really seal a tree wound? Indeed, could slathering a cut with wound dressing be doing more harm than good? It seems true tree recovery requires a much simpler approach. Let’s set the record straight once and for all…

To understand why tree wound sealants became a thing in the first place, there’s a simple (and admittedly silly) explanation. We are prone to anthropomorphism, which means that we think all life forms are prone to reacting like us. So we project our own biological experiences onto plants and wildlife. People once imagined tree wounds needed sealing because they assumed that trees heal like humans, basically.

When a person suffers a deep scrape or laceration, the protocol is clear: clean the cut, stop the bleeding, apply antiseptic ointment, and seal the opening to block external pathogens while our cells heal. Gardeners back in the day figured trees would also need a protective Band-Aid to keep tree sap in and bugs and disease out. When a heavy limb snapped in a summer gale or was lopped off during seasonal pruning, the exposed heartwood looked vulnerable, and any sap seemed alarming.

Gardeners made the mistake of thinking that if they left this tree damage exposed to the elements, wood-boring beetles could march right in, airborne fungal spores might colonize the moist sapwood, and the tree would might bleed to death. By the early 20th century, several petroleum-based asphalt paints, chemical tar compounds, and thick sealants were marketed as miracle aids for healing. The problem? Beneath those seemingly protective layers, the reality was far from protective.

It wasn't until the late 20th century that arborists and tree scientists found that routine sealants can cause more harm than good. They ran rigorous, controlled trials on tree wound dressings and they found that painting tree wounds does not prevent decay or add protection. In study after study, sealed wounds rotted faster and suffered more internal structural breakdown than wounds left exposed to the open air.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Today, leading forestry institutions and the International Society of Arboriculture (ISA) advise against the routine application of wound paints and sealants. The core problem is that wound dressings alter the microclimate of the cut surface. Asphalt paints and sealants dry into an imperfect crust. As the tree barks expand and contracts in shifting weather and humidity, the paint hairline-cracks. Rainwater seeps into these tiny fissures, but the sealant prevents that moisture from evaporating.

When you apply sealant on a tree wound, it traps water inside the wound, allowing bacteria to thrive and fungi to cause decay. The sealant also impedes the tree’s natural healing process. Thick dressings physically smother living plant cells along wound margins, impairing the tree's ability to produce vital callus tissue. By attempting to protect the wound, growers may seal pathogens inside the tree, while locking out the fresh air that recovery demands.

That’s not to say you can’t help out a stressed tree. There are amendments you can add at the ground level to help tree roots with the process of recovery. For example, a light sprinkling of mycorrhizal fungi can assist with rejuvenation. You can buy PureMyco Mycorrhizal Fungi Root Inoculant from Amazon to encourage root growth in stressed trees. But in terms of the trunk or branch, the general opinion now is that clean, unsealed tree cuts heal best on their own.

It’s rare to find a general rule without exceptions. This new expert opinion that sealant should not be used for most tree wounds also has a few exceptions. There are a couple of scientifically backed occasions where dressings can be an essential defense. These exceptions do not exist to help the tree heal faster. Rather, they serve as a barrier to protect specific species against insect-borne epidemics.

The primary time when you might use a sealant safely involves native oak species and elms. In regions where oak wilt or Dutch elm disease are prevalent, fresh pruning cuts or storm tears can result in a leaking sap that attracts beetles that spread deadly diseases like oak wilt and Dutch elm disease. If an oak or elm suffers accidental storm breakage or requires emergency trimming during the high-risk growing season (spring through mid-summer), It’s wise to apply a very thin layer of plain, water-based latex paint or specialized tree wound spray over the cut surface.

A safe sealant option in this case is Tanglefoot Tree Sealant Aerosol, available from Walmart, which is beneficial for emergency summer cuts on oak and elm. The goal is to mask the scent of sap from foraging beetles. Once outside this active insect window, even oaks and elms should be pruned cleanly and left unpainted.

To understand why artificial sealants are generally unnecessary, just bear in mind that trees do not heal like animals do. Trees don’t have the same circulatory system that humans do. Human wounds need closing to prevent loss of bloom, but trees don’t have these issues. Instead, when you prune a tree, the tree initiates a process called tree compartmentalization.

Research led by USDA Forest Service plant pathologist Dr Alex Shigo revealed that trees cannot replace or regenerate damaged heartwood. Instead, they build walls to seal off injured tissue from the rest of the tree. This is called compartmentalization of decay in trees (CODIT). The moment a branch is severed, the tree activates an internal defense consisting of multiple boundaries. Simultaneously, the outer edges of the wound produce swollen ridges of tissue known as callus wood.

Trees start compartmentalizing as soon as you prune them. Cells near the cut area form a cork layer between the wound and the healthy wood inside. Cork is dense and moisture-resistant and quickly forms a natural dressing. At the same time as the tree starts building a callus around the wound, the edge of the cut starts making healthy tissue. This new wood starts growing on the outside, but continues inward until the entire cut surface is covered. This can take years, but ultimately the wound is overgrown. And it works best if you leave the cut alone and let the tree manage it.

Because trees rely on specialized anatomical structures to build their natural defense walls, your pruning technique matters far more than anything that comes out of a can. Proper cuts empower the tree’s natural CODIT defense system, while improper cuts compromise its defenses. Make sure you always use sharp, sterilized pruners or saws. The sharper the blades, the cleaner the cuts. If you need a hand saw, the Fiskars 10-Inch Folding Soft Grip Handsaw, available from Walmart, gives a good grip when cutting through thicker tree branches.

Always cut outside the branch collar when pruning. Look for the junction where a limb meets the parent branch or trunk. The swollen shoulder of textured wood is the branch collar. This collar is packed with cells hardwired to generate those CODIT barrier walls. Make your cut just outside this swollen collar. Never make a flush cut against the trunk, as slicing into the collar invites trunk rot. Don’t leave a 6-inch (15cm) dead branch protruding from the trunk, either, as this is also damaging. The tree cannot compartmentalize dead tissue inches away from the collar.

Large branches are heavy and prone to tearing the trunk if cut from the top. To prevent this, first make a shallow upward cut on the underside of the limb, about 12 inches (30cm) from the trunk. Cut one-third of the way through. Then from above, cut through the limb from the other direction, 2-3 inches (5-8cm) out from the first cut. The branch should break cleanly between the cuts without tearing bark. Finally, make a single, clean cut just outside the branch collar to remove the stub. Once you’re done, leave the cut bare and allow the fresh wood to dry and air-heal.

Storms can rip major limbs from trees, leaving jagged stumps and stripped bark. The secret to storm recovery is acting quickly to clean up jagged breaks so those natural compartmentalization mechanisms can engage. First, never approach trees that are tangled in utility lines or have hanging widow-maker branches suspended overhead. Call professional utility crews or an ISA-certified arborist for high-canopy work.

Always wear safety equipment like a hard hat, safety glasses and sturdy gloves. And avoid uprooted trees or split trunks. They could shift in the wind and fall. After that, assess the damage and determine what can be saved. Wind often twists branches off, tearing strips of living bark down the trunk. Using a sharp utility knife or hand chisel, trim away any loose, jagged flaps of bark, creating a smooth, clean margin around the wound. Keep the healthy inner cambium intact.

Jagged, splintered branch stumps cannot seal properly. Trace the shattered limb back to the nearest healthy branch union or just outside the branch collar, and make a clean, flat saw cut. If a storm strips more than 50% of a tree's canopy, or if the main trunk has split down the center, structural recovery is unlikely. However, if more than half of the canopy remains intact, the tree possesses sufficient power to compartmentalize the damage and rebuild its crown over several seasons.

Pruned or storm-stressed trees need moisture rather than fertilizer. Apply a 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of organic wood mulch over the roots, keeping it 6 inches (15cm) away from the trunk flare. Our team favorite is Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help regulate ground conditions and retain moisture to support damaged trees.

It can be difficult to resist the urge to bandage a damaged tree, especially when a favorite suffers a traumatic break. But these tree-loving insights can hopefully give you the confidence to step back a bit and let Mother Nature lend a helping hand. Trees are ancient, resilient entities, equipped with extraordinary internal defense mechanisms that have preserved them beautifully for many, many years. So skip artificial wound dressings and focus on making precise cuts outside the branch collar, smoothing ragged storm tears, and supporting root health with mulch and consistent hydration, and you’ll give your trees the ability to heal themselves.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7930. Quick Takes With: Kate Berry

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Kate Berry is a creative powerhouse. A floral designer in her past life, she can whip up a gorgeous centerpiece with utter ease. During her tenure as editor-at-large for Martha Stewart Living, she mastered both the glue gun and the piping bag. Later, as the chief creative officer at Domino, she learned exactly what goes into making an artful home. Now the U.S. editor-in-chief of Cabana Magazine, Kate can add one more skill to her resume: wallpaper designer.

The multi-talent recently launched her “Garden in the Sky” collection of wallpapers for Graham & Brown. It’s inspired by her lush 16th-floor terrace garden in the heart of Midtown Manhattan. “The launch has been very satisfying for me. Three wallpaper designs with Graham & Brown, including a climbing branches pattern and an espalier motif, both pulling directly from my terrace garden. It’s been really rewarding to translate something so personal —my own outdoor space— into something people can bring into their homes,” she says.

Below, the plant lover shares one formative memory involving an apricot tree, one tragedy involving a fig tree, one lesson learned from Martha Stewart, and other gardening stories.

We moved a lot when I was growing up, but my mom always planted Vietnamese herbs wherever we lived. I would watch her tend to those little garden beds as if she were a farmer working her fields back in Vietnam. One house, in particular, has stayed with me. We had peach, plum, cherry, and apricot trees, and I was especially drawn to the apricot tree with its beautiful umbrella-like canopy. As a suburban kid with long summers (and no screens), I’d spend hours lying beneath its branches, eating apricots from the tree. They remain the most delicious apricots I’ve ever tasted. Those memories are so deeply embedded in my mind that I can still recall every detail: the warm golden skins dusted with coral-red freckles, their perfect round heart shapes, and their incredible fragrance. It’s one of my happiest childhood memories.

My gardener and designer friends @francespalmer @jduncancampbell. [Read Frances Palmer’s Quick Takes here.]

Untamed, bountiful and lush—which is really the same instinct I brought to designing “Garden in the Sky,” my wallpaper collection with Graham & Brown. I wanted that same lived-in, slightly wild feeling, just translated onto a wall. The collection is named after my terrace garden, which has always felt like my own little slice of nature above the city.

Oh so many but for fragrance, I’d have to say Jasminum sambac.

I mean, I don’t hate any plants but my least favorites would be peace lilies and pothos. They make me think of bad office plants.

I didn’t wrap my fig trees properly and they froze to death this past winter. I feel terrible about it.

To each their own. Are there any bad trends?

Martha Stewart has a bunch of blueberry bushes that produce these giant and tasty blueberries. I’m convinced it’s because of the coffee grounds she feeds them.

Surry Gardens in Maine and Logee’s in CT.

I have plants and trees and style them in clusters at different heights within my apartment to mimic the outdoors. I will add a touch of the garden to meals we have indoors, too—a sprig of lemon verbena or mint in a glass water bottle, or herbs as a centerpiece. And if you’re into wallpaper, that’s the ultimate way to bring the outdoors in through the walls. Its actually what led me to design my wallpaper collection.

I love witnessing the transformation from flower to fruit. It’s incredibly satisfying to watch this process and then be able to pick that fruit. I just love it.

Thanks so much, Kate! (You can follow her on Instagram @nygardeninthesky and @kateberryberry.)

This kitchen gives new meaning to “hearth of the home.”

Situated on an island in Georgian Bay, Ontario, the space is centered on a generously sized stone island. “The family has a tradition of standing and sharing food around the kitchen island on weekends,” says Adam Robinson of Montreal-based Bureau Tempo, who collaborated with Thom Fougere Studio on the interiors of the new build. “We sought to bookend these two important rituals architecturally through the use of stone.”

Unusually, the kitchen island is clad in locally-sourced fieldstone that brings warmth to the otherwise clean-lined space. “We aimed to capture a bit of that rough, wild nature within the interior,” Adam says.

Photography by Alex Lesage, except where noted.

For a look at the rest of the house, see Pine Island Cottage: A Refined (and Appealingly Rough) Lake House on Georgian Bay. And for more by Bureau Tempo, see On a Bustling Brooklyn Street, Above a Busy Restaurant, Quiet Tranquility Inside an Industrial Loft.

Before the recycling goes out, pull a few things aside. Cardboard boxes, old sheets, milk jugs, and more can carry plants through a light frost for free.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Frost warnings in October can seem to arrive with barely a day's notice. One evening, the forecast dips toward freezing while the peppers are still loaded and the fall lettuce is finally filling out. Good frost protection on a night like that doesn't have to come from a garden center.

Before buying frost cloth, take a look in the recycling bin. Last week's delivery boxes, milk jugs, and newspapers can protect plants from frost for a night or two, and the old bedsheet in the linen closet will cover a whole bed of peppers.

There's a limit to what cardboard and cotton can do. They'll carry plants through a light frost, the kind that whitens the lawn at dawn and is gone by mid-morning, but not a freeze that sits in for days. First frosts are often followed by weeks of mild weather, though, and getting tender crops past that one night can stretch the harvest.

So why does a thin bedsheet make any difference? On a clear, calm night, the soil gives off the heat it soaked up during the day, and with no clouds overhead, that warmth drifts up and away. Covers catch some of it on the way out. Drape yours loosely so the edges reach the ground, and the stems have some air space – Home Depot sells steel grow tunnel hoops with a row cover for lifting fabric over a whole garden bed.

Once the air warms above freezing in the morning, the covers need to come off, or they'll trap heat and moisture around the plant. Plastic is the riskiest material here. Wherever it presses against leaves, it carries the cold straight through, so it belongs on a frame or over a fabric layer, never directly on foliage. An analog outdoor thermometer, like this one from Walmart, hung near the garden, makes the morning check easier, though air at ground level can run a few degrees colder on still nights.

Stash these as they come through the house, and keep them dry until a frost advisory goes out.

Flip a box over the plant at dusk. If the cardboard presses on the tips of a young shrub or pepper plant, go up a size and fold the flaps inward so the edges rest on the soil. Container herbs can go under one too. Set a brick on top if there's any wind in the forecast, since an empty box weighs next to nothing. Cardboard also blocks every bit of light and turns soft in heavy dew. It needs to come off first thing in the morning.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A queen-size flat sheet will stretch over a good length of border. Save pillowcases for the odd small plant. By morning, a cotton sheet is often heavy with dew, and stakes or tomato cages pushed into the bed first keep that weight off tender stems. Rocks along the hem will hold it, or you can snap a few row cover clamps from Home Depot onto the stakes. A tarp over the top helps on rainy nights, as long as none of that plastic touches leaves.

Cut the bottom off a gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it becomes a mini cloche for a seedling or a young head of lettuce. That's the same idea behind the reusable plastic cloche from Walmart, though a rinsed jug costs nothing. Press the open edge an inch or so (2.5cm) into the soil to keep it from blowing over, and leave the cap on for cold nights. Twist the cap off on sunny days to let heat escape – a sealed jug in full sun warms up fast.

On a frosty night, the roots in a patio pot sit only a pot wall away from the cold air, while roots in the ground have soil all around them. Bubble wrap taped around the outside of the pot, below the rim, gives them a layer of trapped air to slow heat loss. Since the wrap never touches the plant, it can stay on through a stretch of cold weather, and pots pushed together against a sheltered wall hold their warmth a little better.

If you can't save up enough bubble wrap for your plants, then it's worth picking up a roll of Amazon Basics bubble wrap.

If there's newspaper around the house, spread a few sections several layers thick over low, tender plants and young vegetables, or roll one sheet into a cone for a single seedling. Weigh the corners with rocks or a scoop of soil. Once the dew soaks in, paper loses much of its insulating value. Take it off in the morning and let it dry. On wetter nights, a polypropylene frost blanket, like this one from Home Depot, holds up better.

Rake the leaves into a pile and leave them there for now. Once the soil has cooled in late fall, a few inches heaped around a tender perennial will insulate its crown and roots, though they won't help the foliage. Spread too early, and a leaf layer keeps the ground warm and can give voles a spot to settle in. Shred the leaves with a mower first or a leaf mulcher, like this Worx one from Amazon – the pieces stay loose and drain well – and leave a small gap around each stem so the crown doesn't sit wet all winter.

Slide a whole toilet paper tube, or a third of a paper towel tube, over a seedling or young transplant and push it about an inch (2.5cm) into the soil. That little collar stops cutworms such as the black cutworm (Agrotis ipsilon) from chewing through the stem at the soil line, and it takes some of the bite out of a cold wind, too. Tubes won't do much against frost by themselves, though, so pair them with a milk jug or newspaper on cold nights.

Boxes in the garage and old sheets in the closet can carry a garden through those first chilly nights. Pull the covers each morning, fold them up, and they'll be ready the next time the forecast drops. With a little luck, a few more peppers will ripen before the season wraps up.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7927. The 4 Ps: What to Do in the Garden in November

All Gardenista stories—from garden tours and expert advice to hand tools and furniture roundups.

Starting from scratch or upgrading an outdoor space? Look here for advice on plants and hardscape materials. We have 200 guides on everything from fences to foxgloves.

Heading somewhere? Plan your trip with our destination guides to our favorite public gardens, hotels, restaurants, and shops.

Gardenista’s members-only directory of landscape architects and garden designers.

See our obsessively curated catalog of favorite products sourced by the Gardenista editors.

Happy November! True, most tender annuals are done by now, and some tender perennials are showing signs of cold damage. But even if the more joyful aspects of gardening are past, there is still work to be done in the garden.

The chores for November fall into four categories, which handily all start with “p”: pruning (neatening up), protecting, propagating (and planting), and planning.

Featured image above by Frank Heijligers, from Expert Advice: 9 Tips for a Moody Winter Garden.

Once the leaves have dropped from your trees and shrubs and they’ve entered dormancy, it’s time to remove diseased or damaged branches (with trees, you should consider hiring an arborist) and evaluate their structures. That said, make sure the plant is not among those that shouldn’t be pruned until after they flower in spring. (See Your First Garden: What You Need to Know Before You Prune Shrubs and Trees.) Other plants that need to be cut back include certain berries (pruning out old canes will help the plant rejuvenate next year) and annual plants, which can be snipped down to the soil line, allowing the decaying roots to enrich the soil. But don’t get too hung up on neatness: Consider leaving perennials as they are, withered and brown, for overwintering insects and birds. And fallen leaves should be left in beds to return nutrients to the soil, hold moisture, and provide cover to beneficial insects. (For more on this topic, see Fall Gardening: 15 Ideas For What to Do With All Those Leaves.)

Depending on your location, you may need to help your non-cold-hardy plants survive.This means digging up dahlias and cannas once the top growth is killed by frost, and storing them for the winter (see DIY: How to Store Dahlia Tubers in Winter). And some plants, like fig trees, newly planted trees, or tropical ferns, may need to be covered to survive the winter. (See Garden Hacks: 10 Genius Ideas to Keep Plants Warm in Winter.) Other perennials can use that protective layer of leaves to moderate both temperature and moisture over the winter months.

Transplanting in the fall is easier on the plants due to the cooler temperatures and coming dormancy. Their need for water is reduced during the fall since the cooler temps means less evaporation and dormancy means slow growth. This makes transplant shock far less likely, and the roots will grow until the ground freezes. Now is also the perfect time to take hardwood cuttings of figs and elderberries plants to propagate. Last, save some seeds. While some should be left for the winter birds, saving seeds helps promote a closed loop ecosystem and saves money.

The beginning of November is a perfect time to plan for next year’s garden. The summer is still a recent enough memory and the year-end holidays haven’t yet started. What worked? What didn’t? Maybe the Joe Pye weed was too tall and needs to be moved in the spring? Or maybe you finally figured out where to plant the lavender so that it survived and thrived? Maybe you’ve decided to upgrade your tools and treat yourself to a few that will last a lifetime? And then there are the catalogs that seem to come earlier and earlier every year. There is no happier joy in gardening than the joy of possibilities. As the days grow shorter and colder, the thoughts of all the possibilities for next year are sometimes what we need to get us through winter.

N.B.: This post was first published November 2024.

As the growing season winds down, some plants benefit from a final tidy-up. But knowing what to cut – and what to leave alone – is crucial.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While the cold weather and dropped leaves of November make it seem as if the gardening season is over, there’s still one task left: pruning. Certain plants benefit from a pre-winter trim, while others shouldn’t be touched with pruners until next year.

Some perennials should be cut back all the way right now, while other types of plants, like fruiting vines and certain shrubs, can be touched up more lightly. Exact timing for these tasks depends on your location, weather, and the plant.

Here, we’ll outline some late fall pruning basics and list some of the plants you can tidy up or trim back now, before winter fully takes hold. We also share which plants are better trimmed next season.

Peonies are notoriously susceptible to fungal diseases. The deciduous foliage will die back in fall and, if left in place, can allow fungal spores to overwinter and reinfect plants next year. Trim back foliage once the leaves have yellowed or browned, or earlier if they look diseased.

November is the right time for this chore in many places, but if you garden in a warmer climate, the timing might be later. Remove all of the foliage without cutting it too close to the plant’s crown.

Another herbaceous perennial common in many gardens, hostas die back in fall. Clearing away the spent foliage tidies up beds, makes spring cleaning easier, and prevents many pests and diseases from overwintering and spreading. Cut leaves back to the base without getting too close to or cutting into the crowns. As long as leaves are still green, keep them in place to collect energy. Wait until they die back.

Gardeners are often tempted to cut back the leaves of these early bloomers soon after flowering, but it’s important to wait. The green leaves continue collecting energy to store for next year’s flowers. As long as they are healthy, keep the leaves in place until they start dying back in fall. November is a typical time for pruning bearded irises in many gardens. Cut the fans back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As with irises, you don’t want to trim back leaves just because the plants have finished flowering. Let healthy, green leaves stay in place to gather energy. For many gardeners, daylily leaves will be ready to cut back by November. In warmer climates, you might not trim them back until December. Cut daylily leaves back to a few inches above the ground.

Summer-fruiting raspberries develop fruit on canes that are two years old. Once they’re done fruiting, these older canes use up energy that the plant could be using on new canes and next year’s fruit. Identify the older, woodier canes that fruited this year, and trim them back to the ground.

You’ll also see newer, greener canes. Do not cut these back, or you’ll lose next year’s berries. Tie them together or to a support, like a fence, to protect them from winter winds.

Grapevines need regular pruning to maintain their size and structure and to support abundant fruit production. Timing is important. The vines should be dormant, so they don’t lose too much sap or sprout fresh growth. You also don’t want to prune too late, after hard freezes turn vines too brittle to make clean cuts.

When you find the right time to prune your grapevines, remove dead, damaged, or poorly positioned vines and canes. Identify healthy, young vines and trim around these. Don’t remove all older wood, especially the main trunk and arms.

Lavender hedges that are cold-hardy, like English lavender, benefit from a late fall or early winter trim to maintain their shape and health and protect them from winter weather. Too much material left on the plants can accumulate snow and ice that damage the crowns. Trim these lavenders back by about a third before the real freezing weather begins.

Pro gardeners can't get enough of Felco pruners – and these scored top in our testing.

This handy sharpener keeps pruners in top condition for clean cuts.

This telescopic tool is brilliant for trimming trees and tall climbers – no ladders required.

While these are examples of plants you can and should tackle this time of year, there are also plants that should not be trimmed now.

As a good general rule, you can trim back damaged, dead, or diseased stems and branches from any plant at any time of year. However, harder maintenance pruning needs careful timing. These plants are examples of those that can take a hard trim as winter is about to set in. Most importantly, know which plants and varieties you have and what the best practices are for these before you begin any pruning project.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A plant frost jacket is such a simple, straightforward way to keep plants alive and well over winter, and modern designs with drawstring bases and ventilating zips make it easier than ever to use them. When winterizing a garden, zippered plant jackets don’t only protect tender beauties like banana plants and tree ferns but can help to stop sensitive souls like olive trees from dropping their leaves in a cold snap, shield citrus trees from the occasional frost if you garden in zone 9, and prevent palms from rotting.

Fleece plant covers are also incredibly useful to cocoon early-blooming shrubs like camellia and magnolia if a frost hits just as they’re setting their buds, so you can save the flower show. Young fruit trees, too, can benefit from this extra layer to stop their thin bark splitting in freezing winter conditions, and a plant cover can shield all sorts of other plants from damage caused by snow, sleet and strong winds.

So, if you're getting ready to winterize plants as you prepare your garden for the onset of cold weather, plant jackets should be part of your plan. Not all fleece plant covers are created equal, however, so if you want them to actually work, you need to take a close look at their weight rating. The material used to make frost jackets comes in different weights and, just like comforters offer various levels of warmth, that directly impacts how well it will protect plants in winter, but also the more sunshine it'll block.

Horticultural fleece is a non-woven material typically made from polypropylene, and its weight determines how much protection it offers your plant, measured in grams per square meter (gsm) or ounces per square yard (oz/sq yd). Check the label or online description to find the rating. Any good-quality frost jacket will state the rating and the higher the number, the more insulation it will provide but also block more sunlight.

Armed with this knowledge, you can choose the exact right level of protection for whatever plant you’re winterizing in your USDA zone. While you need to ensure your plant is getting the right level of cold protection, you also need to cater for its sunlight needs.

Because these plants are dormant through winter in colder zones, they don’t need sunlight so you can safely use an ultra heavy-weight fleece to protect them. The fleece alone won’t be enough to protect banana plants (Musa basjoo) and tree ferns (Dicksonia antarctica) from the deep chill of colder zones but are still useful as a cover once you’ve packed layers of insulating straw around the plant. Not only will the fleece form a great barrier against wind and rain but it’ll keep the straw in place and that wrapped plant looking tidy.

Made from 95gsm or 2.8oz/sq yd non-woven material, these plant covers have rounded tops for a good fit and come in green, beige or white in four sizes: 31" x 25", 47" x 39", 71" x 47" and 94" x 79".

Because deciduous shrubs drop their leaves in fall, they don’t need any sunlight over winter to survive so you can safely zip them up in a heavy or ultra heavy-weight plant jacket, depending on the level of protection needed in your zone. This thicker material will also keep snow from weighing down and snapping brittle winter branches. Do choose a design with a zipper as well as a base drawstring so you can regularly open up the zip on milder days to let air circulate.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In 60gsm or 1.77oz/sq yd non-woven fabric, these zippered plant jackets are made of a minimum 50% recycled material and come in four sizes: 23" x 23", 39" x 31", 71" x 47" and 83" x 71".

Hardy shrubs that flower early in the spring such as camellias and magnolias are typically tough enough to survive most winters without a jacket, but their flowerbuds are quickly killed by a late frost or cold snap. Throw on a medium- or heavy-weight plant jacket overnight to save those new buds from the frost.

Evergreen plants such as conifers still need sunlight and fresh air to survive through winter, so a medium-weight fleece is your best bet for general winterizing if your aim is to shield a hardy plant from snow, hail and wind damage. If you’re planning on leaving it on permanently through winter, use a medium-duty fleece for more tender evergreen olive and citrus trees and certain palms, too.

However, if you live in a colder climate you’ll need the increased protection of a heavy- or ultra heavy-weight fleece for these more tender plants. Either use this as an extra layer to throw on over the top of the permanent medium-weight layer in severe weather or, if you use this as the mainstay cover, you’ll need to keep unzipping it to allow sunshine and air in during milder daytime temperatures.

Most medium-duty fleeces are designed without a zipper but that’s not a problem: because the thinner material lets more air and sunlight through, they can safely be left in place.

Made of 32gsm or 0.95oz/sq yd breathable material, this medium-weight plant cover has a drawstring base and is available in three sizes: 32" x 32", 55" x 48" and 72" x 72".

No fleece jacket can generate heat, it can only insulate from the cold, so how you use it has a huge impact on how effectively it protects your plant in winter. Choose a design with both a drawstring and a zip as this not only makes the jacket quick and easy to pop on, but allows you to fit it closely and avoids the wind ripping it off.

Wherever possible, peg the plant jacket to the ground to catch any heat rising upwards. Soil holds onto considerable warmth from the sun, so make use of this natural radiator. Use bricks or stones to weigh the jacket base down, or peg it to the ground with landscape fabric pegs, choosing a product with gaskets to prevent the fabric tearing like these Galvanized Landscape Pins from Amazon.

Similarly, if you’re winterizing a plant in a container, use a frost jacket that’s big enough to fit around the pot, too, as this will protect the roots as well as trap any heat from the soil. Roots in planters are very vulnerable to freezing temperatures so consider wrapping the pot with bubble wrap first.

To prevent moisture building up under the cover and causing mold, make sure you buy a jacket marked as breathable, and open the zip on mild days to allow air to circulate.

While you don’t want to squash a plant into a cover, it’s a wise idea to fit the jacket around the plant to prevent it flapping in the wind and metal greenhouse clamps such as these from Amazon are invaluable to gather loose material or clip a jacket to existing plant supports.

Measuring 8’ x 8’ to fit bigger shrubs and trees, this ultra heavy-weight 80gsm or 2.4oz/yd cover comes with ties and stakes so it can be pinned securely to the ground in exposed gardens.

These ultra heavy-weight zippered covers are made from 75gsm or 2.2oz/sq yd patterned fabric and are available in a green or grey print in sizes 32"x24", 47"x32", 71"x47" and 83"x71".

Shaped for wide, bushy shrubs, this heavy-weight plant cover made of 50gsm or 1.5oz/sq yd fabric measures a generous 7' x 7' and is also available in an 8' square size.

#7924. Man Arrested and Charged for Role in Plotting to Conduct a Mass-Shooting Event in Support of ISIS at the Mall of America

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, of Richfield, Minnesota, was charged today by complaint with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit a federal crime of terrorism.

The FBI arrested the defendant on Oct. 6, and he made his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Elizabeth Cowan Wright on Oct. 7.

“This individual allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Once again this FBI is moving more effectively than we ever have before at stopping terrorists before they can attack Americans – with over 1,100 individuals prevented from conducting attacks, over 4,000 foreign terrorist organization related disruptions and arrests, a 38% increase, and more. We will continue to use every resource we have to detect and prevent acts of terrorism and wipe out their networks all over the country. Thank you to FBI Minneapolis who did an outstanding job in the investigation and likely saved lives.”

“Mohamud allegedly sought to carry out a mass-casualty shooting at the Mall of America, expressing a desire to emulate some of the most horrific ISIS-inspired attacks in the United States, including the atrocities at Pulse Nightclub and 2025 New Year’s Day attack in New Orleans,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will continue to work closely with the FBI and Joint Terrorism Task Force to track down and prosecute ISIS-inspired terrorists in the United States.”

“As alleged in the criminal complaint, Mohamud took substantial steps to plot to murder innocent people in the name of ISIS,” said U.S. Attorney Daniel N. Rosen for the District of Minnesota. “Such threats are taken seriously, and I commend the committed public servants of the Joint Terrorism Task Force, the FBI, and my office, who work every day to stop them.”

According to the complaint, beginning in or about December 2024, Mohamud exchanged hundreds of messages through multiple social media and messaging applications with a confidential source. Mohamud expressed his desire to travel to Somalia to join a designated foreign terrorist organization to fight on its behalf. Mohamud also expressed a desire to commit a mass-casualty event in Minnesota by acquiring and using a firearm and ammunition. The defendant stated many times that if he was unable to travel overseas because of a lack of funds, he planned to carry out a mass-casualty event in Minnesota in support of ISIS.

In July 2026, Mohamud sent messages discussing his intent to carry out a mass-casualty shooting attack at the Mall of America because he claimed it was owned by Jews. He wrote that wanted to kill 30 to 60 people so no one would go there.

In August and September 2026, Mohamud continued to send messages discussing his intentions, including his plans to purchase a firearm and to recruit others to join him in committing the attack. Mohamud sent a selfie-style video of himself pledging allegiance to ISIS:

During the course of his communications, Mohamud stated that he wanted to commit an attack similar to those of the Pulse Nightclub mass-shooting in Orlando, the Bondi Beach mass-shooting in Australia, and the New Year’s Day vehicle-ramming attack in New Orleans.

In September 2026, Mohamud expressed a desire to kill “kuffar” — a term used to refer to a non-Muslim. Mohamud identified Oct. 24 as the date of his planned attack. When the confidential source asked if there was a big gathering on Oct. 24, Mohamud indicated that there were would be numerous Asians and other “kuffar” celebrating at the Mall of America. Mohamud then sent a link to a “Hmong Arts Celebration” at the Mall of America.

In September 2026, Mohamud continued to send propaganda videos to the confidential source. A still shot from one of the propaganda videos sent by Mohamud is depicted below:

On Oct. 6, the FBI arranged to sell to Mohamud, through an undercover FBI employee, an AK-47 assault rifle, four 30-round magazines, and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition. The FBI rendered the AK-47 rifle inert prior to the transaction. The FBI arrested Mohamud shortly after he paid about $600 cash for the rifle, magazines, and ammunition and had those items in his possession. During the sale of the firearm and ammunition, Mohamud reaffirmed his plan to use the firearm and ammunition to shoot people at the Mall of America.

This case was the result of an investigation by the FBI, the Joint Terrorism Task Force, and the Bloomington Police Department, with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigation.

This case is being prosecuted by Trial Attorney Ryan White of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Bejar for the District of Minnesota.

A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7923. Heartleaf Skullcap: A Deer-Resistant Native Perennial

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Amy Galloway Medley shares heartleaf skullcap, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

One of my favorite native species right now is heartleaf skullcap. The fuzzy, heart-shaped leaves are beautiful, and they produce an oil that makes the plant very deer resistant. It looks fantastic planted in masses in a perennial border, with spikes of blue-purple flowers that are similar to those of salvias (Salvia spp. and cvs., Zones 5–11) and that attract hummingbirds.

Some claim that heartleaf skullcap is aggressive, but I find it doesn’t over-compete or crowd anything if you use it for filling those trouble areas where nothing else will grow. In central Texas, most of our native plants prefer full, scorching sun, but this is one that thrives and blooms in dry shade. It’s also impressively cold hardy and makes a wonderful container plant.

Learn more from Amy about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Amy Galloway Medley is the lead horticulturist at Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

#7921. Wild Bleeding Heart: A Hardworking and Adaptable Beauty

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Melissa Starkey shares about wild bleeding heart, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants to grow.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

This plant is extremely close to my heart because I remember seeing it growing wild in Pennsylvania when I was a child. A great alternative to nonnative common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis and cvs., Zones 3–9), it produces its best flush of heart-shaped flowers in spring but keeps blooming through the entire growing season, even as late as November here at Mt. Cuba Center. Wild bleeding heart also has fernlike foliage, which has a kind of blush tinge.

But all its aesthetic qualities aside, wild bleeding heart is incredibly hardworking and adaptable. It can grow in partial shade and makes an excellent woodland plant. This plant also does quite well out in the sun; it grows naturally on rocky, sunny outcrops. I have seen it growing right out of rocks in the wild. While it does adapt well, its unique flowers require larger pollinators, like bumblebees, that are strong enough to force themselves through its tight petals.

Wild bleeding heart is a bit smaller than common bleeding heart, but it does not go dormant like its nonnative relatives, giving you three seasons of interest. If pink flowers aren’t to your taste, there is a white cultivar available called ‘Alba’ (D. eximia ‘Alba’, Zones 3–9).

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.
